#9085. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy® at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Hawaii saver availability on United can be tight, especially during peak travel periods. Here's your playbook:

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy® transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#9083. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#9082. What is at stake for Spain’s art sector as snap election approaches?

A picture of Santiago Abascal, the leader of far-right party Vox, is displayed at the official launch of his election campaign on 13 November

Spain’s snap elections, due to take place on 29 November, have left several long-awaited new measures and legislation for art and culture hanging in the balance. These include regulations on AI, intellectual property and artist welfare. With a coalition between the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party looking increasingly likely, here is what the vote could mean for the country’s art and culture sector.

The future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election. PP has argued in favour of maintaining it, albeit merged with other portfolios, but Vox will only support the ministry’s existence if cultural powers currently held by Spain’s autonomous communities are transferred to the central government.

The prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections. At a party meeting on 22 November, Vox’s secretary general, Ignacio Garriga, stated that they will support cultural professionals who “create quality national products” and “highlight the value of the country's culture”.

Even if the ministry of culture continues, the sector expects budget cuts under a PP-Vox coalition. The PP has pledged to quickly pass a new patronage law with tax and legal incentives to encourage private businesses and individuals to fund cultural projects, arguing that healthcare and defence spending will leave culture underfunded by the state. The PP's proposals for culture also include auditing working conditions, exhibition standards and security protocols across national museums.

The Status of the Artist bill, a welfare package designed to improve working conditions of those in the cultural sector, will enter into force in 2027 regardless of the election results, after being approved by the Council of Ministers in July. However, the inclusion of visual artists—who, unlike other types of artists, were entirely left out of the bill and continue to face prohibitive self-employment quotas—remains up in the air.

Earlier this year, the Union of Contemporary Artists of Spain launched a campaign to push for their inclusion with the support of the ministry of culture, but the decision stalled in the ministries of social security and finance. Gloria Reguero, the president of the union, says that they have been waiting since 2018 for painters, sculptors and photographers to be recognised as artists. “Just when it seemed we were going to start negotiating our terms, the elections came along, and with them, another setback,” she tells The Art Newspaper.

Meanwhile, a separate draft bill regulating the use of generative AI in the arts is not getting off the ground at all. The legislation was put out for public consultation in late September and it marked the government’s third attempt to regulate AI in the arts following two failed royal decrees. The draft bill sought to prohibit the use of generative AI to exploit an artist’s image, voice or work without their express consent and specific remuneration and, like the Status of the Artist, it left out the visual arts.

Both PP and Vox have strongly opposed plans by Ernest Urtasun, the current Spanish culture minister, to review state museum collections—specifically the Museum of the Americas and the National Museum of Anthropology—to “move past a colonial framework”. When the initiative was first announced in early 2024, the PP dismissed the push for decolonisation, in a statement, as “a false debate, imposed and manufactured to create division among Spaniards”.

In November 2025, the ministry formally presented a €13.6m project to overhaul the permanent exhibitions and narratives of both institutions through an “anti-racist and gender perspective”.

Ahead of the elections, the project has reached different stages: while the National Museum of Anthropology has already moved through its public tendering process for the remodelling of its permanent exhibition, the Museum of the Americas remains at an earlier stage, with major works still pending. If a new government takes office, the initiative’s long-term completion, scheduled for 2028, faces significant uncertainty—with a risk that yet-to-be-contracted tenders may be halted or that curatorial direction may be revised. A spokesperson for the Museum of the Americas declined to respond to The Art Newspaper's request for comment, “especially now that we’re on the eve of the elections and everything is so uncertain”, they say.

Tax mandates pertaining to the acquisition of art will be eased for both donors and foundations

CD Projekt Red staff and Naughty Dog's Michael Barclay are among the developers reacting to GTA 6's record 99 Metascore.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 has been out for less than a week, and it isn't just players and critics who are losing their minds. I gave it 5/5 in my GTA 6 review, and it holds a 99 Metascore, tying Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever. As more people play and see more of Leonida, other game developers (those who really know what's what) are lining up to say they're a bit rattled.

The most dramatic reaction I've read came from Igor Sarzyński, creative director on Cyberpunk 2. Reported on Shift Delete, he posted on Bluesky on Saturday evening, two days after launch, and started with "GTA VI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real", then called it "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history" and "a technological and creative miracle".

He joked that Cyberpunk 2 was cancelled and he was off to sweep leaves in his garden.

As our sister site GamesRadar+ covered, Sarzyński isn't the only CD Projekt Red game dev impressed. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski called the game a masterpiece and said it's "unbelievably hard" to achieve what Rockstar has. Cyberpunk 2 associate game director Paweł Sasko called it a "generational banger". Witcher 4 director Sebastian Kalemba said he'd love to lose a whole weekend to it, although he's busy hunting monsters for now.

@RockstarGames created a masterpiece that I am planning to explore in the coming weeks and months. Massive congratulations to the whole team who worked on the game. It is unbelievably hard to achieve what you just did. Hats off to all of youNovember 19, 2026

Over at Naughty Dog, Michael Barclay, who has 19 years in the industry and is working on Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, said GTA 6 looks to him like "a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child".

Push Square picked up on how Barclay was impressed by the lighting specifically, which he explained is mostly dynamic, yet he says it looks as good as, if not better than, most baked lighting. That's a big deal in an open world where the weather and time of day never stop changing.

Tim Soret of Odd Tales (The Last Night) joined the thread, saying he can't work out how Rockstar gets so many draw calls, hair simulations and volumetric lights running at once.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

I’ve made video games for 19 years and GTA VI appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child.November 20, 2026

None of this surprises anyone who's seen how Rockstar builds its world. As I reported earlier, Rockstar's art team designs buildings by imagining who actually lives in them. And then there's the fact that the animators spend months on small details, like how Lucia opens a door with her hip in a natural way when her hands are full.

VP of art Miriam Bellard says they ask whether a place is messy or tidy, and "what is their taste?" The range runs from industrial and scruffy to decadent and dangerous.

So it seems the people who made GTA 6 are as stunned as everyone else by what they've achieved. As GamesRadar+ reported, Rockstar production coordinator Navya Manaswitha reacted to the reviews by saying she's "truly grateful to be a part of this masterpiece".

#9078. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

P.S. Check in with a healthcare provider if you’re unsure when it’s safe to start exercising again.

#9077. Artist Nick Cave and India pavilion win Venice Biennale prizes following controversy

Photo: Marco Zorzanello. Courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia

The Venice Biennale has named the American artist Nick Cave and India’s national pavilion as the winners of its top art prizes this year, following a controversy that saw the competition’s jury resign and several artists and pavilions withdraw from the running.

In previous editions of the Biennale, an international jury has selected the artist and national pavilion to receive the prizes, traditionally known as Golden Lions. This year, however, the awards were renamed Visitors’ Lions and awarded on the basis of votes cast by visitors to the exhibition.

The new voting system was introduced following a dispute over the inclusion of Russia and Israel in the 2026 Biennale. In a statement in April, the five-person jury announced that it would not award prizes to national pavilions or artists from countries whose leaders were charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The International Criminal Court had issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, in 2023, and for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, the following year.

The jurors resigned days later, saying they were doing so “in acknowledgement” of their previous statement.

Dozens of artists then ruled themselves out of the contest in solidarity with the jury, though they remained on the ballot. The Biennale clarified that votes for withdrawn entries would not be considered.

It is unclear whether Cave and the India pavilion received the most votes of all entries on the ballot, including withdrawn entries. The Biennale declined to provide The Art Newspaper with a breakdown of the results.

“The Venice Biennale does not publish rankings or detailed voting results, as the regulations do not provide for this,” a Biennale spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper. “This applies to the Visitors’ Lions, just as it has always applied to the decisions of the international juries.”

Cave is best known for work that combines fashion, sculpture and performance. His exhibition at Venice’s Arsenal includes seven works, among them Amalgam (Origin) (2024), a monumental bronze sculpture of a figure with branches growing out of its body and birds nestling among twigs. Each of the seven works address a stage of grief.

"On the eve of Thanksgiving, I feel an even deeper sense of gratitude, for the friendship that bound me with Koyo Kouoh, and for the fact that she decided to include my work in the In Minor Keys exhibition," Cave said in a statement. "This project is a synthesis of my wider artistic research: it recognises the history of violence and oppression that Black people have endured and continue to endure in the United States, and it pays tribute to the beauty created by that very community, expressing the possibility of growth towards a different future."

India's exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance, features works by five artists including clay sculptures, dried flowers and plants hung from the ceiling, and a demolished family home reconstructed in white thread. Curated by Amin Jaffer, the exhibition reflects on the rapid expansion of cities in India, according to the Biennale's website.

Installation view of India’s pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale, Geographies of Distance: remembering home

Photo: Jacopo Salvi. Courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia

On Wednesday, when this year's winners were announced, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, the Biennale’s president, praised the new voting system.

He said in a statement: “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition—the Visitors’ Award—as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it".

The five-person jury resigned amid an escalating dispute over the participation of Israel and Russia at this year’s Biennale

#9075. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Product placement might not be the same under Pattinson's tenure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond and brings with him a host of luxury deals and an audience that’s grown up alongside him. Matt Kerr, Global Executive Creative Director at Marks, shares what he feels brands will need to do to belong in his version of Bond’s world.

Robert Pattinson has only just got the coveted job as the most famous secret agent on earth, and there’s already speculation around who’ll cut his first dinner jacket. Craig wore Tom Ford, but Pattinson has enjoyed a longstanding relationship with Dior. I’m interested in who gets the job, of course – but I’d like to see what Pattinson does in the suit first.

There’s a little bit of danger in Pattinson’s acting. He has this laid-back British cool thing going on, but there’s also a bit of an awkward edge to him – he’s a bit of a conundrum, and I’d s say there’s something of Fleming’s Bond in that. So, for an agency taking a brief or a brand handing one out, I’d start there. What would this particular Bond choose, and when would we get to see why he chose it?

Fleming was deliberate in showcasing what Bond would buy – he understood his protagonist and the pleasure his audience would get from finding out. The Sea Island cotton shirt, the Rolex, the Aston Martin. You could read the books as a shopping list for a certain idea of British masculinity. The list was interesting because it belonged to a man who had his reasons for choosing things.

Take the silver Aston Martin in Goldfinger. An iconic scene is Bond flipping open the top of the gearstick and sending his passenger through the roof. I couldn’t tell you how long the badge was in shot. But the car still got the punchline. Yes, you can hand over some serious investment to get your car brand into a Bond film, but it’s the association with the scene and the interaction with the hero that people buy into.

I’d give a watch brand the same brief. For No Time to Die, Omega developed the Seamaster Diver 300M 007 Edition with input from Daniel Craig and the filmmakers, then put it on sale to the public. Craig wanted a lightweight watch that felt right for a military man, so Omega made it in titanium. That’s where I’d start with Pattinson too. Work out what his Bond would choose and why. If the audience can see why he’d wear it, they’ve got a reason to want one for themselves.

Brands also need to think about the audience. Yes, Bond is the ultimate masculine icon, but Pattinson is an icon to women in their thirties because they grew up with him. For the teen girl who saw the first Twilight movie at 15, Pattinson is her pin-up. And if he stays with the franchise for the best part of a decade – which seems to be the norm – that young girl will be in her forties. So, I’d have that in mind when I was briefing the campaign.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Take a hotel partnership. There’s a familiar version of that ad where a man books a weekend so he can spend it feeling like Bond. According to Nielsen data, women influence 70 to 80% of consumer spending, so maybe brands should ask what a hotel brand could offer a woman who has followed Pattinson for years and fancies booking the weekend herself. Give her a detail to spot at check-in and let it pay off later that evening. She gets to have some of the fun Bond has in the film. If the partnership carries through to another film, the hotel can give her something different to come back for.

I’d keep the gun barrel iconography and every word of the slick one-liner, “Bond, James Bond”, but I’d give Pattinson room to play with the pause. We know the line so well that we’ll hear the difference. And I’d make this the rule for every brand partner. Make it make sense for Bond but show me what makes it right for Pattinson’s Bond.

When the first design concepts come in, I’d put my thumb over the 007 mark. If the cufflink shot underneath could sell any Saville Row suit, I’d send the team back to the drawing board. It must fit this new era of Bond - something that Craig’s or Connery’s might have passed on.

Some of the old partnerships will still fit. Others will need to go or evolve with the way he plays Bond and the audience that will spend the next decade watching him. For a brand planning its next five to ten years, the next Bond film might be the last great monoculture event.

Matt Kerr is a Global Executive Creative Director at Marks with more than 20 years’ experience shaping brands and leading creative teams. His work spans brand identity, packaging, campaigns and digital experiences for clients including LEGO, Diageo, Reckitt and Haleon. At Marks, he has helped transform the agency’s strategic design offering and leads creative standards across a global community of more than 500 designers.

#9073. Christie’s Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio

Christie’s has added the UK auction house Dreweatts to its portfolio.

In a statement on Wednesday, Christie’s chief executive Bonnie Brennan said that the auction house has long admired Dreweatts. “Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service. Both businesses will continue to operate much as they do today, while building on their respective strengths and the significant opportunities we see for future growth,” she said. Related Articles Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds Yoshitomo Nara Painting Fetches $15.9 M., Outselling Koons and Richter in New York

Dreweatts specializes in single-owner collections and country house sales, ranging from furniture and works of art, old masters, modern and contemporary art, Asian and European ceramics, modern design, jewelry, silver, luxury accessories, clocks and wine. The auction house was founded in 1759 by Thomas Davis, a cabinetmaker, upholsterer and land agent from Abingdon, Oxfordshire. Dreweatts operates its main salesroom from its country house, Donnington Priory, in Newbury, Berkshire, and also has a showroom in London on Pall Mall.

Henry House, chief executive of Dreweatts, said in a statement that under this new arrangement “we can use the additional advantage of one another’s expertise to better serve our buyers and sellers. Dreweatts has had a parent company before, which enabled us to grow the business and prosper, and this move is an extension of that model.” He added that the Christie’s acquisition provides certainty for the auction house and that Dreweatts will continue, under his and chairman Will Richards’ stewardship.

Christie’s president of EMEA, Anthea Peers, said that the François Pinault-owned auction house recognized Dreweatts as a “healthy, compatible business to our own and the value it can add to what we do for all of our clients.”

On November 19, Dreweatts presented its Fine Watches & Luxury Accessories auction that totaled £529,934 with an 89% sell-through rate. The sale included fine watches, designer handbags, writing instruments and luxury objects from Patek Philippe, Cartier, Hermès, Chanel and Montblanc. The top lots were a Lange & Söhne that sold for £49,780 and a Montblanc black porcelain fountain pen that sold for £8,320.

#9072. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Senior Games designer James Wyatt explains how 50+ artists were blended into one Azeroth for D&D: World of Warcraft.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This month, two imaginary worlds collide as the legendary tabletop roleplaying game Dungeons & Dragons joins forces with the wildly popular MMORPG, World of Warcraft.The two fantasy franchises have crossed paths before, albeit obliquely, with Warcraft: The Roleplaying Game in 2003, a standalone RPG that was compatible with D&D's 3rd Edition ruleset. The upcoming D&D: World of Warcraft gameplay expansion book, however, is the first full-blooded crossover to bring the different species, settings and magical items of Warcraft to the beloved D&D 5E ruleset. "It's such an obvious partnership that it was only a matter of time before it finally happened," admits Senior Game Designer James Wyatt, who led the project for D&D publishers' Wizards of the Coast. "Fundamentally, this book is about playing D&D in the world of Azeroth, and giving you the tools you need to do that."

D&D: World of Warcraft is a lavish 256-page hardback book that takes you back to the magical realm of Azeroth and enables you to explore it in the context of your D&D games. The new volume contains 13 WoW-themed character classes for you and your friends to play as, including staples such as Death Knights and Druids, Warlocks and Warriors. It's also chock full of lore that will enable you to devise a rich background for your characters, as well as a wide range of professions and gear that will help them on their adventures. "I like to tell players that they can make a character whose backstory is unique, entirely unlike any other character with the same species," says Wyatt, of the book's flexibility. "You can play a Night Elf with the Sailor background, perhaps having grown up ferrying passengers between Auberdine and Rut'theran, never venturing into the heights of Teldrassil – unlike every Night Elf in the MMO. Or you might choose the Entertainer background for your Orc, deciding that you were part of a small, unloved theater company in Orgrimmar for years before deciding to seek your fortune as an adventurer instead. The possibilities are limitless!"

The new book contains a wealth of new illustrations alongside art that has been carefully selected from World of Warcraft's vast archives. "When I came in, I was like, okay, do we have the resources to do this all from scratch, or are we picking out some of the art [from the archives]?" says Jaramillo. "From there it was about figuring out which artists we would have and what type of visuals we would like to include, because World of Warcraft has several different styles of illustration, right from the beginning, like Chris Metzen's sketches [most of which hail from the early, pre-MMO versions of Warcraft – ed.] and then going through the Alex Horley work to more modern stuff, with Billy Christian and Andrey Kuzinskiy." In total the book contains work by more than 50 artists. In terms of the methods and materials used, the book was a real mix with Jaramillo stating that, while most of the artists worked in PhotoShop and Procreate, some painted with oils and then touched the images up digitally.

In short, it's a perfect blend of these two iconic games, though adapting an online game into a pen and paper RPG was no simple task. "Different parts of the game presented very different challenges," says Wyatt. "And even each WoW class demanded a different set of solutions as we tried to express that class in D&D terms. The result is a book that I think pushes our design across the board to new levels, and challenges our team to continue to innovate and explore the reaches of what we can do in D&D design."Of course, ImagineFX is first and foremost a digital art magazine and we're excited about the visuals in the book as much as we are the game itself. D&D: World of Warcraft does not disappoint on that level – it's a genuinely lavish affair, with every chapter filled with gorgeous, evocative images that celebrate World of Warcraft's long history. Art Director Sergio Jaramillo led the design of the book in what sounds like a dream gig for the veteran WoW player."I joined the D&D team around two years ago," he explains. "By that time [Wizards of the Coast and WoW-owners Blizzard] were already thinking about getting this project prepped. As I was joining the team, my creative director asked me, 'Is there anything that we're working on that you might be interested in?' and immediately I said, 'Warcraft!' That is my jam. I was very familiar with the world, so it was a no-brainer for me."

Another consideration that the art team needed to bear in mind was that Dungeons & Dragons books have an established format. "We had to have a visual UX layout," says Jaramillo. "The experience of the book needs to feel like it's a D&D book. With the chapter opener images, if it's a class [chapter] then it needs to feel like that class. The species pages need to inform what different types of characters you might find in a species." So, for example, the image used to illustrate the section on the Orcs is rendered in reds and greens, to reflect the creatures’ different skin tones in the video game. Sometimes, however, a hole would need to be filled with the creation of an all-new image. "For the professions we found a [picture of] a guide fishing, but we needed at least one Horde image too, so that it didn't look like we're skewed towards just the Alliance," Jaramillo explains. "So we added an image of an undead gathering some shrooms. It was a case of getting the right images that we needed for the game. We had access to all these gorgeous pieces of art and we definitely dug deep into the archives of Blizzard."

Of course, a big part of the appeal of both Dungeons & Dragons and Warcraft is losing yourself in a richly-detailed fantasy world. The locations of Azeroth remain a vital part of the WoW experience, arguably more so in this tabletop form where players are relying on the imagination of their DM, rather than graphics, to guide them through an adventure. To help make the dungeons accurate to the game, Wyatt played through the MMORPG's various dungeons, trying to map them out, while Jaramillo worked with cartographers Damien Mammoliti and Marc Moureau. "Their style of art is a little bit different," says Jaramillo. Mark is a bit more comic book-ish, in the work that he does, it's more lines, and Damien is very painterly. So it was like, OK, how do we make these maps and styles look similar and inform [the players] that they belong to World of Warcraft. So we put them on parchment that is very reminiscent of the WoW maps. That's the bridge between these two artists and between D&D and WoW."

One of the earliest locations that players will encounter in the book is the dank Blackfathom Deeps, a fallen temple of Elune that has been defiled by the sinister Twilight's Hammer, evil worshippers of the Old Gods. It's Wyatt's favourite dungeon in the book."Blackfathom Deeps holds a special place in my heart for a couple of reasons," he says. "My first WoW character was a Night Elf, and I spent months steeped in the aesthetic of the Night Elf regions of the world, including Teldrassil, Darkshore, and Ashenvale (where Blackfathom Deeps is located). I love the colors, the landscapes, and the music of those regions, and the hints of the sweeping history of the Night Elves I got as I adventured through those areas. It was also one of the only dungeons that I actually played as part of a group in those early years, where mostly I was exploring the world solo or with my daughter."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Wyatt hopes that D&D players who have never experienced the MMORPG before will find inspiration for their own campaigns. "Any of the monsters in the bestiary chapter of this book can be dropped into a D&D campaign on any world," he notes. "My hope is that D&D players who pick up this book will realize that Azeroth is a really cool world that has a lot to offer as a setting for D&D campaigns!"And as for those gamers who grew up with WoW and who are coming to D&D for the first time? "I want them to recognize the feeling of being in Azeroth, almost like you were sitting down and hearing the 'Legends of Azeroth' main title for the first time again. And then at the same time to realize with delight that this is an opportunity to explore the world in a whole new way. This is an Azeroth where you can talk to anyone you meet, interact with anything you see, go anywhere you want to, and try anything you can imagine. I can't wait to hear about the stories our players and DMs tell with this material."

When it comes to selecting Sergio Jaramillo's favourite image from D&D: World of Warcraft, the Art Director says that he cannot pick just one from the wealth of gorgeous visuals contained in the new book. "I'll give you three instead," he laughs. "One from the species, one from miscellaneous stuff, and one from the final characters in the book." From the species, Jaramillo chooses an old WoW favourite. "I have to go with the image of the Pandaren. That piece, as soon as it came in, I was like, 'Oh, this just feels right.'"When it comes to the miscellaneous pile, he chooses something more imposing. "I would have to go with the only new class image that we commissioned for the book, the Dracthyr Evoker," he says of a glorious picture of a fearsome and imposing dragon painted by Andrey Kuzinskiy. "That's just great. I really love the energy in that piece."Finally, for the characters, he chooses an image by Alex Horley of a character known in the game as 'the daughter of the sea'. "I think it would have to be the picture of Jaina Proudmoore. Alex just did a really amazing job on that piece."

As you might expect, Easter eggs for both games are littered throughout the new book, though both Jaramillo and Wyatt are coy about where you might find them. "The Easter Egg Hunt is less exciting if I tell you where to find them," says the latter, though he points to the piece of art used to illustrate the sections on mounts and companion creatures, noting "The mount and the companion should be recognizable" to fans."I wish I had more time to add even more Easter eggs to this," says Jaramillo. Asked for an example of one that he did manage to sneak in, he highlights a neat nod to D&D. "The art that we picked for the warlock class chapter is of a Gnome. That was just perfect because our warlock art in the D&D book is also a Gnome. So it's like okay, that’s nice. It just fits."

D&D: World of Warcraft is published by Wizards of the Coast, and is out now.

Will Salmon is Tom’s Guide’s Collections Editor. He has been writing about film, TV, comics, tabletop games and music for almost 20 years, which is quite a long time if you stop and think about it. At Future he launched the scary movie magazine Horrorville, relaunched Comic Heroes, and has written for every issue of SFX magazine for well over a decade. His music writing has appeared in The Quietus, MOJO, Electronic Sound, Clash, and loads of other places too.

#9070. Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire

An abandoned warehouse at the doomed Fordlândia industrial settlement Sipa USA/Alamy Stock Photo

Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia. A once bustling—albeit highly exploitative—village, it was established by the US industrialist Henry Ford in the 1920s. Fordlândia’s sole purpose was to serve as a rubber-tapping enterprise that would provide materials for the Ford Motor Company. But less than a decade after its founding, the rubber crops failed. With the development of synthetic rubber following close behind, Ford abandoned the project in 1945, and the village along the Tapajós River fell into severe disrepair.

Earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution. Local and national authorities have until the end of this month to come up with a conservation plan.

Ford’s company originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927. He envisioned building a Midwestern-style village as a hub for latex extraction, supplying materials for his factories in Michigan. Ford hoped to upend the dominance of British-controlled rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, which had left US manufacturers dependent on foreign suppliers.

Fordlândia, beyond giving the Ford Motor Company control over its supply of raw materials, was imagined as a self-sufficient settlement for around 10,000 people in the Amazon. Ford himself viewed Fordlândia as a sociological experiment intended to “Americanise” the local population, although the tycoon never visited his dystopian village. Workers there, many of them Indigenous people and migrants from northeastern Brazil, endured cultural subjugation and often faced dangerous conditions—including having to work through the hottest part of the day. Hundreds of people died during the short-lived project.

Workers organised a mutiny in 1930 after unreasonable restrictions were imposed in Fordlândia, including the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco, as well as the requirement of US customs like square dancing and a diet of wholewheat bread, brown rice, oatmeal and canned peaches. Shortly afterwards there was a full-scale riot, in which workers chased their American managers and the village cook into the jungle. The Brazilian army was brought in to restore order. The company subsequently fired a number of workers and appointed a new manager to complete Fordlândia’s infrastructure. (An agreement on serving different food to the workers was also reached.)

Fordlândia Dance Hall, around 1933 The Collections of the Henry Ford

Ford’s social experiment unfolded alongside agricultural problems. Without the consultation of local experts, the rubber trees had been planted too close together. This made them vulnerable to disease and pests, and the growing conditions along the river were unsuitable. In 1933, at the recommendation of the American plant pathologist James Robert Weir, a second plantation was established downstream at Belterra, where conditions were more appropriate. Although it fared better than Fordlândia, production remained costly and it never became commercially viable.

No usable latex was ever produced in Fordlândia. After investing millions of dollars with no return, Ford sold the land back to the Brazilian government. The population dropped by more than 90% in the following years, but squatters and families moved back into the decaying structures in the 2000s. Around 3,000 people live in Fordlândia today, even as the village remains unconnected to paved roads.

The federal process for the designation of Fordlândia as a heritage site has been unresolved since the 1990s, when the move was first suggested by local advocates. In 2015, Brazil’s federal public prosecutor’s office filed a lawsuit stating that the site had “unquestionable” cultural value. In 2024, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage (Iphan) countered that Fordlândia lacked the criteria required for federal heritage listing, pointing to the loss of its original characteristics and the site’s deteriorated condition.

But in May 2026 a federal court ruled that, even without formal heritage status, the site should be protected. This decision was based on a 1988 constitutional article that mandates the conservation of both material and immaterial assets connected to Brazilian communities. The court added that uncertainty over ownership of the site had been used repeatedly as justification for inaction, and that the state of Pará and the municipality of Aveiro (which administers Fordlândia) had previously signed an agreement to begin conservation measures that never materialised. It also alleged that some interventions had been carried out without authorisation.

A Fordlândia sawmill in 1931, before the Ford Motor Company’s rubber-plantation project was halted The Collections of the Henry Ford

The court ruled that Iphan must now work with the state and municipality to deliver a plan by the end of November 2026, outlining the responsibilities of each government entity and the needs of each site in Fordlândia—including emergency measures for structures at imminent risk. Once approved, conservation work must begin within 30 days. If deadlines are not met, the court will impose a daily fine of $2,000 (10,000 reais) on the federal government and Iphan, and a $1,000 (5,000 reais) fine on the state and municipality. Iphan must also begin the administrative process to recognise Fordlândia as a heritage site.

In a statement to The Art Newspaper, a spokesperson for Iphan says the agency does not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. It remains unclear if Iphan plans to counter the court’s decision. “In May 2024, Iphan’s cultural-heritage advisory council denied Fordlândia’s designation as Brazilian cultural heritage,” the spokesperson says. “Iphan reiterates that it remains committed to the preservation of Brazilian cultural heritage, as mandated by the constitution.”

The sites to be reviewed include the former Fordlândia Hospital, designed by the Detroit architect Albert Kahn; the long-abandoned industrial and port warehouses; the houses of the American Village, where the company’s American managers lived; the workers’ village; the Henry Ford School; the Cine Patinha, a cinema whose roof has recently collapsed; and a convent on a cliff overlooking the Tapajós River, built in the post-Ford era and active until the early 2010s. All these structures have been exposed to the Amazon’s heat, humidity and heavy rainfall for years.

Fordlândia remains highly remote, receiving few outside visitors and requiring a minimum six-hour trip to reach via high-speed boat. Still, there is evidence that intrepid travellers have made the journey. A company specialising in tours of the Amazon is currently offering a five-day visit to the region, including a stop in Fordlândia, for approximately $3,000 (16,000 reais) per person. Reviews for “Fordlândia Ghost Town” on TripAdvisor average 4.7 out of 5 stars, with one reviewer in 2016 calling the site “historical, magical and melancholic”, and another saying it tells a story of “hubris, determination, paternalism and ultimately failure”.

Although Fordlândia is unlikely to be commercialised as a tourist destination, the village’s surviving infrastructure has come to represent an unusual and failed attempt to Americanise and industrialise the Amazon. The remnants of the settlement also tell the story of the Brazilian workers who lived there, and those who have continued to inhabit it. The Brazilian government maintains that Fordlândia has “unquestionable historical, cultural and architectural value”, and that it represents “an American attempt to break the British monopoly on rubber and bring modern infrastructure to the middle of the Amazon”.
