#9037. Sid Lee Architecture references "rhythm of the vine" for curved Ontario hotel

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise)

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

#9036. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

Size is the first thing to think about. A 150cm table like the Nordic gives you room for a laptop and a sketchbook at one end, while dinner happens at the other. Alternatively, an extending table like the Buxton lets you go bigger when a project demands it.

Materials matter too. Solid oak, as used by Oak & More and Grain & Frame, can be sanded back and refinished when it picks up the inevitable scratches and paint marks. Veneer is lighter and cheaper, but much less forgiving.

Then there's design. Habitat’s been bringing modern design to the British high street since Terence Conran founded it in 1964, and the Nel shows it still has an eye for detail. Grain & Frame's pared-back Scandi style, meanwhile, will suit those who prefer their furniture to fade quietly into the background.

#9033. Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

#9031. Framery's flexible pod subscription tackles office furniture waste issue

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this issue with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” said Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

According to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#9029. resembling a geometric flower, 10-meter aluminum lookout frames views in australia’s victorian alps

flower of the alpine sun is a monument to the sensational light of the alps, a thoughtful abstraction in dialogue with the surrounding environment.

Gio Veronesi edited by christina vergopoulou November 25, 2026 4 min

Installed at an elevation of 1,750 meters in Falls Creek, within Australia’s Victorian Alps, Flower of the Alpine Sun is a 10-meter-diameter occupiable lookout and public sculpture designed by Gio Veronesi. Unveiled in June 2026 following a 2018 commission by Alpine Resorts Victoria, the Melbourne Prize Trust, and Regional Development Victoria, the project was relocated at Veronesi’s recommendation from a lower parking area to a chairlift-accessible rock outcrop above the village.

Accessible via a pedestrian walkway, the structure by designer Gio Veronesi invites visitors into its interior platform to view the surrounding mountain range through an open geometric lattice. Referencing the alpine sun and the seasonal shift from winter snowfields to summer wildflower meadows, the circular volume reads as a marker on the skyline from the valley below, shifts in profile upon approach, and aligns into a radial frame when viewed from the center of the platform.

A single geometric system governs the structure from overall layout down to individual nodal junctions. Engineered to withstand heavy alpine snow loads and high-altitude winds on the exposed ridge, the primary load-bearing frame and visitor platform are fabricated from galvanized steel. The outer structural frame and cladding elements are constructed from aluminum finished in a custom powder-coated color developed in collaboration with Dulux.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#9027. Bennetts Associates revives Victorian hospital for University of Edinburgh

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

#9026. Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection review: A brilliant slice of gaming history

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection is a fascinating archive of Team17's early years, filled with art and developer insights, even if not all the games deserve a return visit.

Six Amiga-era Alien Breed games in one package

Virtual Museum is packed with art, interviews and unreleased projects

Twin-stick controls, CRT filters and save states

Local co-op, online Rush Mode and solo Horde Mode

The 3D games feel like historical curiosities

Early top-down games can be punishingly difficult

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Format: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, PC

How to buy: Digitally on the PS Store, Xbox Store, Steam

Some games you remember as brilliant, and others you remember as brilliant because you were 12, sitting in front of an Amiga with a joystick in one hand and a pile of floppy disks beside you. Alien Breed is probably a bit of both.

Team17's sci-fi shooter celebrates its 35th anniversary with this new collection, bringing together six games from the series' original Amiga era (read my Apidya review for more Amiga gaming). That's quite a lot of history in one package, taking in the original top-down shooters and the later, more ambitious attempts to bring the series into the 3D era.

And there's a lot to like about the way this collection has been assembled. Alongside the games is an interactive archive filled with original artwork, developer interviews, soundtracks, design documents and even material from Alien Breed projects that never made it to release. It's a proper look back at a British studio finding its feet during one of gaming's most interesting periods.

But one question hangs over it all: are these games still fun to play?

The collection includes Alien Breed (1991), Alien Breed: Special Edition '92, Alien Breed II: The Horror Continues, Alien Breed: Tower Assault, Alien Breed 3D and Alien Breed 3D II: The Killing Grounds.

The first four are the games most people will remember, and I played more of the classic top-down 2D shooters, with their overhead perspective, maze-like levels, and hordes of aliens waiting around every corner. There's a little Gauntlet in the DNA, a bit of Smash TV, and more than a hint of James Cameron's Aliens. You explore abandoned space stations, collect ammunition, hunt for keys, and try not to get overwhelmed by the growing number of creatures closing in, often because of a brutal respawn system.

It's a simple formula, but Team17 – now a publisher of some of the best indie games – knew how to make it entertaining. There's a nice rhythm to working through a level, finding supplies and opening up new areas, although the difficulty can be pretty unforgiving.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Playing those early games now in the 35th Anniversary Collection showcases both the strengths and weaknesses of the series. These games are brutally fun when you take time to learn the maps, play and replay, remember where keys are located, and manage the alien 'breed' and its AI by keeping it locked behind corridor walls.

But it can also become overburdened by the horde; without the right weapons, life is short-lived, and it can be frustrating to waste keys and then not be able to unlock the doors you need, and restart beckons. The original is worse for this; the Special Edition improved, and by Alien Breed II the team had ironed out the kinks, and the game plays with a perfect rhythm. Back in the 90s, we had to play two games and three years to get perfection; on this collection, it's right there.

Some may disagree; I think Alien Breed II, with its visual detail and balanced map design and item placement, is the best of the series, but Tower Assault comes close. The environments offer more variety and a stronger sense of progression, but the second game is the real gem.

Then there's the move into 3D, something I envied back in the day because you needed an Amiga 1200 or Amiga CD32 to run it. Alien Breed 3D arrived in 1995, when everyone wanted to make a Doom-like shooter, and Team17 was keen to prove the Amiga could compete with the growing PC gaming setups and new consoles like PlayStation. It was an ambitious move, especially given the hardware limitations, and the sequel, The Killing Grounds, pushed that idea further but, interestingly, dropped much of the Alien Breed branding and imagery for a more Doom-like aesthetic.

Playing them now is a different experience because a) I can play them and b) they're important games in the story of the Amiga. But being historically interesting and being enjoyable shooters are two very different things.

Alien Breed 3D now feels like a tech demo, and it drops much of the series' identity: the 3D experience. I remember the impact this game had back in '95, especially for Amiga owners used to pushing the computer's graphics to the limit. But is it a good game? Not really. It's a decent Doom clone, but even in '95 it couldn't compete with games like Dark Forces.

Alien Breed 3D II is slightly different, though: it plays better today and has a cleaner, more focused Doom-like appeal, but much of Alien Breed's visual hooks and identity have been ironed out in favour of what feels like a solid, standalone Doom clone.

But playing all the games back to back in the 35th Anniversary Collection is more interesting than just replaying games I loved on my Amiga, because it shows how a series develops, how improvements are inched forward, how trends and pressures pull on a brand and force new directions. This is where the collection excels.

If you're buying this collection purely for the games, you might be missing its biggest selling point.

The Virtual Museum is an interactive archive that lets you explore the history of Alien Breed through original box art, advertising, concept work, soundtracks and interviews with the people who made the games. It also includes a timeline and material from projects that never saw the light of day, which I've spent far more time exploring than I imagined. It includes a cancelled PSP game that looks like it could have struck the right balance between 'modern' 3D and classic Alien Breed corridor shootouts, and an Alien Breed RTS that would have used randomised levels and X-Com-like gameplay.

I love seeing this sort of material included in retro collections. It's easy to throw a few old games into an emulator and call it a day, but preserving gaming history takes more than making sure an old title still runs on a modern console.

Alien Breed was part of Team17's early identity, and this archive gives you a better idea of how the studio developed the series, what it was trying to achieve and how its ambitions changed as gaming moved from 2D to 3D.

The collection includes interviews with the original artists and developers, plus art, models, design docs, and even videos showing concept art progressing from sketch to final painting. Those cancelled games offer a wealth of content rarely seen in retro game collections, including level maps, concept art, and even gameplay demos.

The original games also get welcome additions that make them more accessible. Twin-stick controls are supported across the 2D and 3D titles; you can choose from display formats, CRT filters, and screen bezels, and save states mean you don't have to commit to a full session every time you sit down.

The collection also includes local co-op in supporting games, online Rush Mode and a new solo Horde Mode. These additions are useful, particularly if you want to play with someone else or fancy a more immediate arcade challenge.

I've spent time digging into the setup menus and fiddling around; for example, there's a choice of CRT scanlines, but also scanline transparency levels. There's no remake-versus-original graphics mode, because these aren't remakes but excellent emulations. I find the new DualSense control layout feels right; it's modern without ruining the series' distinct feel, and you still get that Alien Breed thing of hugging corridor walls.

There are some compromises, though. The original games have been preserved in their original formats, and while that's important, it also means some of their limitations come along for the ride. The 3D games in particular will test your patience if you're used to modern shooters because you need to play within the game's little 3D window (it's not as modernised as the Star Wars Dark Forces Remake, for example), and the collection could have done more to make those games 'modern'. But then that's the knife's edge a collection like this runs: we want the games we had 35 years ago, but we expect today's features; we can't have it both ways.

As a fan back in the day, I love having all these games together on a modern console, partly because they're still good, but also because I never got to play the 3D entries. Alien Breed is an important part of Team17's history, and the collection does a good job of showing how the series evolved across six releases.

But I don't think the games themselves have aged equally well. The top-down shooters still have something to offer if you enjoy old-school arcade games, with Alien Breed II being the one I've been returning to more than the others. The 3D games are more difficult to recommend as anything other than historical curiosities.

But it's the archive that makes this collection worthwhile. The artwork, interviews and unreleased projects give Alien Breed a context that simply playing the games can't provide. It's a chance to look at a British studio's creative development over an exciting period for gaming, a time when Team17 could have been swallowed but it thrived, and that's worth celebrating.

If, like me, you grew up with an Amiga, there's plenty here to enjoy. If you've never played Alien Breed before, however, I'd approach it as a piece of gaming history rather than a newly discovered classic because not every game in the collection is a banger.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. #9025. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#9024. Upside-down cantilever cracks open timber hotel by BIG

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”

The hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

#9023. designboom’s guide to miami art week 2026: what to see in and out of the fairs

explore must-see highlights of art basel miami beach, design miami, and other standout shows and events across the city.

Miami Art Week returns from November 30th to December 6th, 2026, bringing a packed program of art fairs, outdoor installations, exhibitions, and unexpected encounters across Miami and Miami Beach. This year, the city becomes a setting for everything from giant mirrored disco balls and interactive robots to surreal theatrical environments and public sculptures built for play. Don’t miss our upcoming Miami Art Week LIVE feed, updated daily with on-the-ground discoveries, highlights, and real-time dispatches from across the city.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns with a reconfigured fair and an expanded digital art program, while Design Miami explores the stories behind collectible objects through its curatorial theme, Unveiling. Beyond the convention center, the Miami Design District welcomes a series of interactive sculptural installations by Objects of Common Interest, and Faena Beach becomes a dance floor beneath a monumental mirrored sphere by Christopher Joshua Benton.

Meanwhile, CJ Hendry invites visitors into a swimming-pool-sized pit of oversized pills, Marcel Dzama brings his dreamlike universe to Lincoln Road, and Miami’s galleries and museums open new exhibitions. From established fairs to temporary interventions along the beachfront, here’s designboom’s guide to what to see across Miami Art Week 2026.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with 272 exhibitors from more than 40 countries and territories. For 2026, the fair introduces a reconfigured floor plan with a smaller overall footprint, longer sightlines, and established international galleries distributed throughout the space alongside younger exhibitors.

The fair’s main sectors bring together contemporary work and historic presentations, with Nova focusing on recently created pieces, Positions supporting emerging artists through solo booths, and Survey revisiting overlooked artistic practices. More than 30 galleries will participate for the first time, with a strong presence from Latin America and the Caribbean.

Zero 10, Art Basel’s platform dedicated to art of the digital era, returns with Generation, an exhibition curated by Karen Archey and Eli Scheinman. Featuring 19 projects, the presentation explores how digital technology is changing the ways art is made and experienced, with works by artists including Refik Anadol and Sarah Meyohas.

what: Art Basel Miami Beach when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Drive, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Design Miami returns for its 22nd edition with more than 75 exhibitors bringing together historic and contemporary collectible design. Under the direction of curator Charlene Prempeh, the 2026 fair follows the theme Unveiling, inviting visitors to look more closely at the cultural histories and making processes behind the objects on display.

The program spans established galleries and emerging practices, with furniture, lighting, and sculptural works presented alongside experimental installations. The fair’s Curio section provides a platform for more focused design presentations, while special projects and collaborations extend the program beyond the traditional gallery booth.

As one of the main events of Miami Art Week, Design Miami brings together designers, collectors, and galleries working across different generations of material experimentation and craftsmanship.

what: Design Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 (invitation-only previews December 1st and 2nd) where: Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach, FL

Untitled Art celebrates its 15th Miami Beach edition with more than 170 galleries and nonprofit organizations representing 36 countries and territories. The fair returns to its beachfront pavilion along Ocean Drive, offering a curated selection of contemporary art with an emphasis on emerging practices and independent galleries.

The 2026 edition features five sectors: Main, Artist Spotlight, Nest, Non-Profit, and Special Projects. Artist Spotlight, curated by Agustina Ferreyra, brings together focused solo presentations, while Nest, curated by Willem Molesworth, explores collaboration and exchange across East Asia and the wider international art scene.

With 53 first-time exhibitors joining the program, the fair continues to create space for younger galleries alongside established international participants.

what: Untitled Art when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Ocean Drive and 12th Street, Miami Beach, FL

The New Art Dealers Alliance returns to Ice Palace Studios for the 24th edition of NADA Miami, bringing together 135 exhibitors from 63 cities and 27 countries.

Known for its focus on independent galleries and emerging artistic practices, NADA presents work from both established and younger art spaces. Its relatively informal setting offers an opportunity to discover artists working across painting, installation, sculpture, and experimental media, with presentations that often take a more exploratory approach than those found at the larger international fairs.

The event occupies Ice Palace Studios in downtown Miami, with exhibitions and programming extending into its outdoor areas.

what: NADA when: December 1st — 5th, 2026 where: Ice Palace Studios, 1400 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33136

Art Miami returns to its waterfront pavilion at One Herald Plaza with an international selection of modern and contemporary art. One of Miami’s longest-running art fairs, the event brings together established galleries presenting works from the 20th and 21st centuries.

The fair spans painting, sculpture, photography, and installation, with a program that moves between historically significant artists and contemporary practices. Alongside conventional gallery presentations, visitors can expect individual artist projects and interactive installations, including a new felt environment by British artist Lucy Sparrow.

Located in downtown Miami, the fair takes place alongside its sister event CONTEXT Art Miami, allowing visitors to move between the two exhibitions.

what: Art Miami when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Running alongside Art Miami, CONTEXT Art Miami returns to One Herald Plaza with a focus on emerging and mid-career contemporary artists. The sister fair brings together 75 international galleries presenting new work and curated solo exhibitions.

Established in 2012, CONTEXT offers a platform for galleries working with younger artists and those developing new approaches to familiar media. The fair also features installations and projects created specifically for the event, offering visitors a view of contemporary practices beyond the more established market represented at Art Miami.

what: CONTEXT Art Miami when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: CONTEXT Art Miami Pavilion, One Herald Plaza, NE 14th Street, Miami, FL 33132

Amsterdam-based Studio DRIFT brings Murmuring Minds to Art Basel Miami Beach’s Zero 10 sector, presented with the digital art platform TAEX. The installation transforms an arena of autonomous robotic blocks into a responsive environment, with their movement shifting according to the actions of visitors.

Entering the space, one person at a time can influence the robots as they move collectively, follow a lead, or behave according to patterns inspired by wind and natural swarms. The project draws on DRIFT’s long-running research into collective behavior, particularly the coordinated movements of birds and other living systems.

The presentation also includes Coded Nature, an interactive digital series in which algorithmically generated swarms respond to visitors’ gestures. Together, the works examine how individual actions influence the behavior of larger systems.

what: Studio DRIFT, Murmuring Minds and Coded Nature when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

At Art Basel’s Zero 10, Sarah Meyohas presents Phase Transition, a new installation of organic, sculptural forms that appear to communicate through movement and sound. Presented by Boesky Gallery, the work brings together magnetized liquid, algorithmic systems, and synthesizers to create a strange conversation among objects.

The forms rest on mesh pedestals or hang from suspended wires. Cutout windows reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing magnetic particles that shift in response to programmed magnets. These movements are translated into sound, allowing each sculpture to participate in an ongoing exchange.

Their rounded, bodily shapes reference biological growth and transformation, while their mechanical conversations raise questions about intelligence and communication beyond human language. The installation extends Meyohas’ interest in the relationship between organic life and emerging technologies.

what: Sarah Meyohas: Phase Transition when: December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2nd — 3rd) where: Art Basel Miami Beach, Zero 10, Miami Beach Convention Center

During Miami Art Week this December, artist Derrick Adams and the LEGO Group will bring a nine-foot unicorn pool float to Miami Beach. Built from LEGO bricks, the oversized figure will sit at the center of Pool Party, a colorful installation at Avant Gallery inside 1111 Lincoln Road. The project takes Adams’ long-running Floaters series, with its images of Black people at leisure, into an entirely different medium.

On December 3rd and 4th, visitors will have a hand in creating the artwork themselves. Adams and the LEGO team will invite the public to help assemble parts of the installation, ahead of its completed unveiling on December 5th. The two-day community build is part of The Art of Building, a participatory experience organized during Miami Art Week — RSVP here!

what: Derrick Adams x LEGO: The Art of Building when: December 3rd — 4th, 2026 (completed installation reveal December 5th) where: Avant Gallery, 1111 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, Florida

Japanese artist Tadashi Kawamata brings a site-specific installation to Collins Park in collaboration with Maison Ruinart during Art Basel Miami Beach. Part of the champagne house’s ongoing Conversations with Nature program, the work draws on Kawamata’s observations of Ruinart’s historic vineyards in France.

Known for his temporary architectural constructions made from lightweight materials, Kawamata approaches installation as a process of responding to a place. His Miami commission continues that interest through a large-scale structure that invites visitors to reconsider their relationship with the surrounding environment.

what: Tadashi Kawamata x Maison Ruinart when: December 3rd — 6th, 2026 where: Collins Park, Miami Beach, FL

Dutch designer Iris van Herpen brings her collaboration with Maison Perrier-Jouët to Design Miami, following its presentation in Tokyo and Paris earlier this year. The project grew from her selection as the inaugural recipient of the Perrier-Jouët Design for Nature Award.

Drawing on cymatics, the study of how vibrations produce visible patterns, van Herpen translated signals associated with the living ecosystem of the champagne house’s vineyards into sculptural forms.

The resulting creations include Symphonic Bloom, a one-of-a-kind artwork made from recycled golden metal and silk surrounding a historic champagne bottle, and Symphonic Life, a limited series of sculptural sleeves adorned with gold. The pieces carry van Herpen’s interest in natural structures into the scale of collectible objects.

what: Iris van Herpen x Maison Perrier-Jouët when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: Design Miami, Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach

British artist Lucy Sparrow returns to Art Miami with The Money Laundry, an interactive installation that transforms a familiar laundromat into a shop filled with handmade felt objects.

Among the colorful boxes of detergent and cleaning supplies, visitors will find painted felt banknotes, imitation luxury watches, and passports created by the artist. Sparrow will also exchange $100 in real money for a bundle of felt currency carrying a fictional value of $600.

An on-site photo booth allows guests to have their own felt passports painted live, extending the artist’s ongoing interest in consumer culture and the objects through which people assign value.

what: Lucy Sparrow: The Money Laundry when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Art Miami, Booth AM207, One Herald Plaza, Miami

Artist Christopher Joshua Benton transforms Faena Beach into a temporary dance floor with A Lore Supreme, a monumental kinetic sculpture that reimagines the disco ball as a map of Miami’s cultural history.

The mirrored sphere rises 27 feet above the sand and stretches 44 feet across. Its surface is composed of around 7,000 reflective facets, which move with the wind and scatter images of the surrounding beach.

Partially embedded in the ground, the sculpture becomes both a gathering place and a setting for music and performance.

Drawing on research into Miami’s musical communities, Benton incorporates recorded conversations and sound from local DJs and musicians. The installation traces the influence of African, Caribbean, and Latin American cultures on the city’s music, turning the beach into an open-air space for listening and dancing.

what: Christopher Joshua Benton: A Lore Supreme when: December 1st — 6th, 2026, noon-9 p.m. where: Faena Beach, 3201 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

The Miami Design District’s 11th Annual Design Commission has been awarded to Objects of Common Interest, the New York- and Athens-based studio founded by Eleni Petaloti and Leonidas Trampoukis.

Titled Out of This World: A Field of Conditions, the installation places six abstract sculptures throughout the neighborhood. Some release clouds of vapor into the Miami air, while others rotate when touched or distort their surroundings through reflective surfaces. A marble-and-resin pyramid produces sound that becomes audible only when visitors approach.

Developed through the studio’s ongoing experiments with resin, marble, and movement, the commission extends into Design Miami with a companion installation, Out of This World: A Certain Attraction. There, a concealed sculptural object responds to the presence of visitors, shifting to reveal fragmented reflections of those who enter.

what: Objects of Common Interest, Out of This World: A Field of Conditions when: during Miami Art Week 2026 (exact opening date to be confirmed) where: various locations throughout the Miami Design District, Miami, FL

Artist Marcel Dzama brings his distinctive universe of masked figures and theatrical imagery to Miami Beach with Who Loves the Moon?, an immersive installation presented by Capital One and The Cultivist.

The experience begins with a giant Moon that opens its mouth to welcome visitors inside. From there, guests move through a series of environments incorporating illuminated optical works, puppetry, and imagery drawn from Dzama’s paintings and films.

The journey culminates in a theatrical landscape with checkerboard floors and towering palms. By day, visitors can play chess and explore tarot and astrological readings. Evening programming introduces music and performances by Miami City Ballet, bringing the artist’s imagined world into motion.

what: Marcel Dzama: Who Loves the Moon? when: December 1st — 4th, 2026 (public hours: December 3rd, 10:30a.m. — 4p.m. / December 4th, 10:30a.m. — 6p.m.) where: 434 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Australian artist CJ Hendry joins Salon 94 Design to bring PASTEL to the Miami Design District, transforming thousands of oversized pills into an immersive landscape of color.

The installation revisits Hendry’s earlier bead-filled environment, this time replacing the familiar spherical forms with sculptural vitamins, supplements, and prescription pills. Visitors can enter the swimming-pool-sized pit, sift through the colorful objects, and assemble their own playful prescriptions.

Through the oversized forms, Hendry turns familiar products associated with health and self-optimization into objects for interaction and play.

what: CJ Hendry x Salon 94 Design: PASTEL Miami when: November 30th — December 20th, 2026 where: 3925 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

At The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, American artist Rachel Lee Hovnanian presents The Perfect Trade-Off, a solo exhibition exploring how technology has changed the ways people spend time together.

In the hotel’s Art Deco lobby, Dinner for Ten stages an elaborate meal with ten places at the table. Nine chairs are occupied by monitors depicting individuals absorbed in their phones, leaving a single empty seat for visitors. As the feast deteriorates, the work considers what happens to shared rituals when attention turns toward digital devices.

The exhibition extends onto the beachfront with Poor Teddy in Memoriam, a monumental bronze teddy bear surrounded by flowers. Elsewhere, a vintage three-wheeled Piaggio Ape has been transformed into a functioning phone-charging station, bringing Hovnanian’s examination of our relationship with technology into a familiar, everyday encounter.

what: Rachel Lee Hovnanian: The Perfect Trade-Off when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: The Ritz-Carlton, South Beach, 1 Lincoln Road, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Argentine artist and designer Andrés Reisinger brings his dreamlike architectural imagery into physical space with Do You Dream In Color?, a property-wide exhibition at Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

Known for his surreal digital environments and all-pink architectural takeovers, Reisinger will transform parts of the hotel through immersive installations and digital artworks. At the entrance, one of his signature draped interventions will cover the architecture in flowing fabric-like forms, while more digital works appear throughout Bar Centro and the hotel’s screens.

The exhibition is presented with ArtRepublic, and brings Reisinger’s digitally conceived aesthetic into an environment that visitors can experience in-person.

what: Andrés Reisinger: Do You Dream In Color? when: December 1st — 6th, 2026 where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Greek designer Natalia Triantafylli presents Under the Libra Sun at Villa Paula in Miami’s Little Haiti neighborhood, marking her first major exhibition and largest-scale work to date. Presented by The Future Perfect, the collection takes inspiration from the historic villa’s original tiles and gardens, with pieces that reinterpret Greek and Victorian ornament through bright colors and floral patterns.

Triantafylli hand-sculpts forms in clay before scanning them and combining them with 3D-printed counterparts. The collection includes two monumental porcelain chandeliers, decorative mirrors, column-capital tables and stools, and her first upholstered pieces. Several works are developed with her partner, artist Andrew Pierce Scott, whose blackened steel structures contrast with her richly patterned ceramics. The pieces are bolted together rather than glued to leave their construction visible.

what: Natalia Triantafylli: Under the Libra Sun, presented by The Future Perfect when: opening November 30th, 2026 where: Villa Paula, 5811 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33127

Bosnian artist Radenko Milak presents Algorithms for the Future at Piero Atchugarry Gallery in Miami, his first solo exhibition in the city. Curated by Claire Breukel, the show brings together hyperrealistic black-and-white watercolors that examine how technology shapes our memories of the past and visions of the future. Drawing from archival photography, science fiction, and architecture, Milak combines familiar imagery with imagined scenarios, from Edward Hopper’s solitary figures to futuristic skyscrapers filled with surveillance equipment.

Among the works is White Noise (2026), which merges a warped urban tower with vintage recording devices, and Ghost Game, a series of 23 paintings tracing the history of artificial intelligence through mathematics, cinema, and popular culture. Each image is painted by hand with near-photographic precision, a deliberately slow process that contrasts with the speed of algorithmically generated pictures. The works question what happens when machines begin to determine how history is represented and remembered.

what: Radenko Milak: Algorithms for the Future, curated by Claire Breukel when: November 29th, 2026 — April 18, 2027 where: Piero Atchugarry Gallery, 5520 NE 4th Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

Design Hotels teams up with Play-Doh for Designed to Play, a five-day program at The Shelborne by Proper in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2026. At its center is an installation by Copenhagen-based Helle Mardahl Studio, created in collaboration with Hasbro’s new Blooms by Play-Doh collection. The project marks an unusual moment for the familiar modeling compound, which has introduced its first line developed specifically for adults in the brand’s 70-year history.

Throughout the week, visitors can experiment with the colorful material in hands-on workshops and create their own sculptural bouquets. The hotel will also host morning conversations on creativity and design, while New York’s Pawn Chess Club brings custom chessboards and open games to the space. The program takes a playful approach to the usual Miami Art Week schedule, with opportunities to make something, try a new game, or simply spend an afternoon experimenting.

what: Design Hotels x Play-Doh, Designed to Play, featuring Helle Mardahl Studio when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026 where: The Shelborne by Proper, 1801 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Miami’s Wynwood Arts District welcomes Grotto Baths on December 1, a 7,500-square-foot social bathhouse that brings contemporary art into the centuries-old tradition of communal bathing. Designed by Antoinette Marie Johnson in collaboration with Stokes Architecture + Design, the interiors draw from Brazilian modernism, with curved archways, geometric tile patterns, and bursts of orange and blue against natural stone and travertine. Visitors move between thermal pools and cold plunges, while a 30-person cedar sauna hosts guided rituals accompanied by aromatic steam.

Art plays a central role in the new space. Miami-based artist Emmett Moore has created site-specific sculptures and custom benches using reclaimed materials inspired by South Florida’s limestone and mid-century breeze-block architecture. Works by Papou appear in the lobby, and an exterior mural by Mandy Ann takes inspiration from water. The phone-free bathhouse also includes a garden café, with special food and drinks inspired by Moore’s installations planned for Miami Art Week.

what: Grotto Baths, featuring site-specific installations by Emmett Moore when: Opens December 1st, 2026, for members (day-pass access begins December 7th) where: Grotto Baths, 325 NW 28th Street, Miami, FL 33127

At Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, Japanese artist and ceramic conservator Naoko Fukumaru presents a collection of works exploring the centuries-old practice of kintsugi, the repair of broken ceramics using lacquer and gold.

Presented in collaboration with The Morikami Museum and Japanese Gardens, the lobby exhibition brings together ceramic objects that have been broken, discarded, or altered through firing. Fukumaru reconstructs their forms using natural urushi lacquer and 23.5-karat gold, leaving visible lines that trace the histories of the objects.

With more than three decades of experience in ceramic conservation, the Kyoto-born artist approaches repair as an opportunity to give damaged objects a new visual identity.

what: Naoko Fukumaru: The Kintsugi Art of Naoko Fukumaru when: November 25th — December 7th, 2026 where: Nobu Hotel Miami Beach, 4525 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

Miami’s Little River neighborhood welcomes a new cultural space with the opening of Mitrani Art, a multidisciplinary center dedicated to photography, video art, and film.

Founded by sisters Dina and Rhonda Mitrani and designed by R&R Studios, the project transforms a former mechanic shop into galleries and artist studios, with a screening room and outdoor courtyard. The opening marks a new chapter for the sisters, who previously operated the Mitrani Warehouse in Wynwood.

The inaugural exhibition, ReExposures: The Magic Within, brings together artists who have contributed to their programs over the years. Works range from large-scale photographic experiments to video installations, including a monumental photogram by Roberto Huarcaya and Antonia Wright’s video Suddenly We Jumped, in which the artist breaks through panes of glass.

what: Mitrani Art, ReExposures: The Magic Within when: Opening November 30th, 2026 (6-9 p.m. reception) where: Mitrani Art, 7325 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33150

The Bass in Miami Beach presents a season of exhibitions that bring visitors into direct contact with the works on view, from interactive environments to sculptural installations.

In the museum’s Rotunda, Argentine artist Amalia Pica presents Lecturas Posibles, an almost two-dimensional library where surfaces become chalkboards. Visitors are invited to write and draw across the installation, creating an evolving collection of marks and messages.

Elsewhere, Japanese artist Yuko Mohri’s Unviolated Imperfection explores everyday objects through unpredictable mechanical systems, while architecture and design duo Pedro y Juana transform an interior with patterned surfaces and custom furniture for Aquí. Their richly colored environment draws on Miami’s subtropical setting, inviting visitors to spend time within the installation.

what: The Bass 2026-2027 exhibition season, featuring Amalia Pica, Yuko Mohri, and Pedro y Juana when: exhibitions on view throughout Miami Art Week 2026 where: Bass Museum of Art, 2100 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33139

LVMH The Studio Miami returns for its sixth edition, bringing a five-day program of contemporary art and creative workshops to the Miami Design District.

The pop-up gallery presents works by ten artists working across painting, sculpture, textiles, photography, and digital media. Participating artists include Cavier Coleman, Glenneisha Darkins, Jay Chung, and Kristen White, alongside others exploring identity and cultural history through different materials.

Alongside the exhibition, visitors can attend public conversations and craftsmanship demonstrations organized with artisans and creative partners from Louis Vuitton, Tiffany & Co., and TAG Heuer.

what: LVMH The Studio Miami 2026 when: December 2nd — 6th, 2026, 11 a.m.-4 p.m. where: Palm Court Event Space, 140 NE 39th Street, 3rd Floor, Miami, FL 33137

The Craig Robins Collection unveils its 2026-2027 rehang, Real Shadows, featuring more than 300 works of modern and contemporary art and design.

Presented at Dacra’s headquarters in the Miami Design District, the exhibition brings together pieces by John Baldessari, Charles Ray, and Marlene Dumas, alongside recent acquisitions by artists including Alex Da Corte and Lauren Halsey.

Taking its title from Baldessari’s Tetrad Series (1999), the exhibition explores the persistence of images through painting and sculpture. The presentation also incorporates significant design objects by Zaha Hadid, Jean Prouvé, and Ron Arad, reflecting the collection’s long-standing relationship between art and furniture.

what: Craig Robins Collection: Real Shadows when: 2026-2027; Wednesdays-Fridays, noon-4 p.m., by appointment where: Dacra Headquarters, 3841 NE 2nd Avenue, Miami, FL 33137

El Espacio 23 in Miami’s Allapattah neighborhood presents Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas, a new exhibition drawn from the Jorge M. Pérez Collection. Bringing together more than 130 works by 120 artists, the exhibition examines the region’s shifting cultural identities through migration and shared histories. Curated through a collaboration between Anelys Alvarez, Patricia Hanna, Taiyana Pimentel, and Patrick Charpenel, the presentation moves between figurative art, political expression, and abstraction.

Among the works is José Carlos Martinat’s kinetic sculpture Manifestos, whose moving pendulums and speakers broadcast historical art manifestos in their original languages. Elsewhere, Hernan Bas revisits Miami’s brief snowfall in 1977, while works by Julio Le Parc and Adrián Villar Rojas explore different approaches to visual language. Across four interconnected sections, the exhibition considers Latin America as a network of relationships that extends far beyond geographical borders.

what: Nothing Is Linear: Relations Across Latin America and Its Diasporas when: November 19th, 2026 — August 14th, 2027 where: El Espacio 23, 2270 NW 23rd Street, Miami, FL 33142

Jeffrey Deitch presents Ensalada Mixta, an exhibition of work by Swiss artist Urs Fischer in the Miami Design District.

The presentation explores Fischer’s approach to transforming familiar objects through unexpected materials and changes in scale. Working across sculpture and design, the artist draws on industrial processes and common domestic forms, using materials including steel, epoxy, and electrical components.

The exhibition continues Fischer’s long-running interest in the relationship between art objects and the everyday things that surround them, bringing his playful visual language into a temporary gallery setting during Miami Art Week.

what: Urs Fischer: Ensalada Mixta, presented by Jeffrey Deitch when: November 30th — December 23rd, 2026 where: 45 NE 39th Street, Miami, FL 33137

At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, Basquiat. A Hidden World offers a new perspective on Jean-Michel Basquiat’s paintings through his little-known use of ultraviolet-reactive materials.

Curated by Dieter Buchhart and Anna Karina Hofbauer, the exhibition brings together four works, including Untitled (Orange Sports Figure) (1982), Emblem (1984), Cash Crop (1984), and O.M.R.A.V.S. (1984).

Under ultraviolet light, words and markings hidden within the surfaces become visible. In Emblem, the repeated phrase ‘invisible men’ appears beneath the familiar composition, revealing an additional layer of Basquiat’s visual language.

what: Basquiat: A Hidden World when: November 29th, 2026 — February 12th, 2027 where: ICA Miami Expansion Space, 23 NE 41st Street, Miami, FL 33137

Indian artist Subodh Kerkar brings The Ocean Odyssey to Miami Beach as a free public performance presented by REEFLINE in collaboration with Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa.

The site-specific project brings together more than 50 community participants and dancers from Miami City Ballet, with choreography developed in collaboration with Durante Verzola.

Taking place directly on the beachfront, the performance uses movement to explore the relationship between people and marine environments. The ocean becomes the setting for a temporary gathering that connects contemporary art with Miami’s coastal landscape.

what: Subodh Kerkar: The Ocean Odyssey, presented by REEFLINE when: December 1st, 2026, 4:30-6 p.m. where: Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa beachfront, 4041 Collins Avenue, Miami Beach, FL 33140

“Imagine not having a photo of your own stadium”.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Logging on to socials today, there's no escaping AI content, and audiences are getting increasingly skilled at sniffing it out. Maybe it's a rogue extra finger, or a reality-warping background that raises alarm bells. But for Crystal Palace fans, a blatant misspelling of their own mascot is what instantly had fans questioning whether there was slop afoot.

Sadly, it's pretty unsurprising, as even huge iconic brands like Coca-Cola have been caught up in AI controversy. With slim regulation and the tools only getting more advanced, it seems AI content isn't slowing down – but neither is the backlash.

We are pleased to confirm that Selhurst Park is a candidate host venue for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035 🦅 https://t.co/EUw5OI8hgGNovember 23, 2026

Announcing that its home stadium, Selhurst Park, is a candidate host for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035, Crystal Palace's seemingly innocent post was pretty unassuming at first. It's only when you take a closer look at the finer details that things get questionable. Excuse me... who are the 'Eacles'?

Fans quickly criticised the design, claiming there was no need for AI in such a simple post. "Do we not have a photo of the f**king stadium, our media team is in the gutter," one dissapointed fan wrote. "Imagine not having a photo of your own stadium and needing to slop one," another added, while one noted, "This is such a basic level of graphic design that would’ve taken seconds to make."

With AI tools readily available and often integrated into our everyday creative software, it's no surprise that it keeps infiltrating our feeds. With brands increasingly squeezed for resources and time, quick AI image generation feels like the obvious choice, but here it risks sacrificing the quality of your content. What should've been a celebratory post about the Women’s World Cup then becomes a source of derision and disappointment, proving that sloppy AI shortcuts aren't without consequence.

For more creative insight, check out why replacing creative jobs with AI could have a hidden cost or take a look at what happens when clients trust AI more than creative expertise.
