#9021. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

This has topped our guide to the best office chairs since we reviewed it over a year ago. It's the best mid-priced chair we've tested, offering an excellent balance of value, good design, comfort and sound ergonomics with a padded, two-way adjustable lumbar support for back health and ample adjustability. Gaming chairs often aren't very ergonomic, or very well built at all, in fact, but the Secretlab Titan Evo was a revelation, with a much more refined design than we expected. Branch’s Multitask chair is the one of the US-based furniture manufacturer’s cheapest offerings, and it strips things down to the fundamentals. There's no lumbar support, but it has a solid build and premium feel for a very reasonable price.

See our full Branch Multitask chair review.

Autonomous make some of the best ergonomic chairs out there, and the Ultra 2 stands out for its resemblance to one of the most popular Herman Miller chairs – and at a much more accessible porice.

See our Autonomous ErgoChair Ultra 2 review

The Hinomi H2 Pro stands out for adjustability. With 19 points of adjustment, it competes with much more expensive chairs and comes out winning. A novel bonus is that it folds down into a compact shape that's easy to tuck away, making it a great pick for anyone short on space.

If you want an office chair that makes more of an interior design statement, the Verve stands out with its sleek, modern lines, 3D-knit back weave and colour-matched frames for a sleek modern look. It has great easily adjustable lumbar support and a nicely balanced recline, but note that the arm rests aren't adjustable.

An office chair with a fan? We thought it was a gimmick, but our reviewer was surprised to find himself won over by the rechargeable Omni Pro with its fan and motorised lumbar support won us over. The motorised adjustment lets you precisely dial in the perfect lumbar position, and the articulated backrest accompanies movement really well.

For a more luxurious traditional leather chair, the X4 Executive stands out as one of the most comfortable chairs we've tested. Combined with the metal base, the leather upholstered sear provides reassuring support.

The quirky Hag Capisco is our favourite office chair for combining with a standing desk. It looks fantastic as a design object, and it's actually surprisingly versatile. you can sit on it like a normal chair, perch on it when you're standing, or turn it around and use the back rest to support your chest instead. This range of options encourages movement through throughout the day between sitting, perching and standing.

So which is the best ergonomic chair Black Friday deal for you? We think the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro offers the best balance of comfort, adjustability and looks, while the Branch Verve stands out for design lovers. The Hinomi H2 Pro is ideal if you're tall or love tweaking every detail. And if you're happy to rethink how you work altogether, the HAG Capisco remains in a class of its own.

But if budget is tight, the Sihoo M18 is an easy pick. We've not found another chair that offers this level of comfort and build for such an economical price: just be aware that you'll need to assemble it.

#9018. "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Hunters Point Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings, both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do – leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

#9017. kanal-centre pompidou opens in brussels inside restored 1930s citroën garage

the new museum combines contemporary art, architecture, performance and more than 20,000 square meters of free public space, proposing a more open relationship between cultural institutions and the city.

Designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium comprising EM2N, noAarchitecten and Sergison Bates architects, Kanal opens in Brussels on November 28th, 2026, transforming a former Citroën garage into a 40,000-square-meter museum and public cultural center (find designboom’s previous coverage here). The project houses contemporary art, architecture, performance, film and community activities under one roof, with over 20,000 square meters of freely accessible public space.

Kanal’s artistic program develops through a long-term partnership with Centre Pompidou, which provides access to one of the world’s leading collections of modern and contemporary art. The collaboration, initiated in 2017, also involves institutional support, exhibition production and joint curatorial work.

Built in 1933–34 on the banks of the Charleroi-Brussels Canal, the former Citroën complex was conceived as a monumental setting for the automobile. Its defining features include a vast glass-and-steel showroom facing the street and an expansive industrial structure behind it. Atelier Kanal restores the existing building and introduces three new structures within it, creating spaces for exhibitions, performances, research and public activities.

The former showroom remains central to the identity of the building, as it retains the scale and openness of its original architecture, taking on a different cultural role. Across its five floors, the museum accommodates exhibition galleries, performance and film auditoriums, workshops, a library, a research center and community spaces. A basement gallery, reaching seven meters in height, adds another dimension to the exhibition program.

A 700-square-meter indoor playground designed by Turner Prize-winning architecture collective Assemble brings another dimension to Kanal’s public program. Conceived as an imaginary landscape, the installation draws inspiration from the piles of coal once transported along the Charleroi-Brussels Canal, reinterpreting this industrial history as a terrain of hills and volcano-like forms. Ropes, tires, masks and other loose elements invite children aged four and above to explore and play.

The playground extends into a dedicated workshop space for movement and encounters between generations. Alongside the museum’s library, bookshop, rooftop terrace and community spaces, it reinforces Kanal’s ambition to function as an everyday public destination.

The opening exhibition, A truly immense journey, brings together more than 350 works dating from the early 20th century to today. Artists include Lygia Clark, Sonia Delaunay, Alberto Giacometti, Natalia Goncharova, Wifredo Lam, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso, alongside contemporary artists such as Sammy Baloji, Edith Dekyndt, Aglaia Konrad and Hana Miletić. Drawn from the collections of Centre Pompidou and Kanal, as well as Belgian and international public and private collections, the exhibition considers how people, ideas and artistic movements have shaped the modern world.

Other opening presentations establish a more locally engaged and multidisciplinary direction. An infinite woman: Black archives in two acts examines how artists of African descent have reclaimed and reinterpreted colonial imagery associated with Mangbetu women from the Congo. Belgian artist Otobong Nkanga’s With These Hands invites visitors to participate in a collective weaving installation, where trained workers and members of the public work side by side, exchanging skills and experiences. The museum also presents new commissions by Belgian artists, including Joëlle Tuerlinckx and Manon de Boer, alongside a free presentation by Banu Cennetoğlu.

Architecture has its own dedicated presence through Kanal Architecture, the new home of the institution formerly known as CIVA, Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, landscape architecture and urbanism. With its own library and research center, the institution develops a program focused on the relationship between the built environment, society and the ecosystems that shape cities.

Its inaugural exhibition, Right to the City – Right to the Future, looks at Brussels as a testing ground for alternative spatial practices and addresses its complicated relationship with modernization, including the large-scale demolitions associated with the Manhattan Plan and their lasting impact on surrounding neighborhoods. Another initiative, Yser Print Coop by WERKER Collective, will establish a cooperative print room inside the museum until the end of 2028, providing space for risography, woodcut and screen printing.

#9016. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#9015. Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the issues that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

If you've been waiting for the right 3D printer deal to start exploring this exciting craft, Black Friday is your moment. The Elegoo Black Friday sale is in full swing, and the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo, a machine we highly recommend for beginners, is reduced by $80 to $369 at Amazon.

We think this is an ideal choice for beginners since it's easy to set up and run, offers good value and provides plenty of flexibility to grow as a creator since it can handle a range of materials and multi-colour printing (see our guide to the best 3D printers to see how it compares to other options we've tested). There are also a couple of great deals running on Elegoo resin printers if you want to make more detailed objects, and the brand's running discounts on resins and filaments.

Hitting the sweet spot for speed, quality and versatility at an accessible price, the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo FDM printer is suitable for everyone from first-time makers to experienced creators. The enclosed CoreXY design, automated setup and leveling, intuitive user interface, 350°C hardened-steel nozzle and four-colour system offer an approachable path into multicolour printing while providing the performance and flexibility to push projects.

The open-frame Centauri 2 is reduced to $279 but the Carbon version's closed frame has the benefit of allowing the use of temperature-sensitive materials such as ABS, ASA, nylon, polycarbonate and carbon fiber filaments

The Saturn 4 is a resin printer for creators who need precise, ultra-fine detail with high surface quality. With a 16K LCD, it offers large build volume, a heated vat, and automatic levelling and tilt-release technology for an efficient workflow ideal for tabletop gaming models, miniatures and collectible characters.

See our full Elegoo Saturn 4 Ultra review.

For a more economical introduction to resin 3D printing, the Mars 5 Ultra is an accessible option for tabletop gamers and miniature enthusiasts. Automatic leveling, tilt release and print-failure detection keep the setup and operation simple, while 9K resolution can deliver detailed results if not as fine as the 16K Saturn 4 Ultra above.

For most beginners, an FDM (fused deposition modeling) 3D printer is the way to go. They're safer, cleaner, cheaper to run, and easier to post-process than resin printers. We recommend the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo because as well as making things as easy as possible, it provides plenty of versatility to dive deep once you're ready to start getting more hands on and to develop in 3D printing, without having to go out an buy another machine that allows more flexibility.

It leaves very little work to do in assembly, with no gantries to bolt together. You just remove the accessories and shipping foam, plug in the screen, and you can be up and running in a few minutes. It offers a practical mid-size build volume of 256 × 256 × 256mm (10.1 × 10.1 × 10.1 inches), the closed frame means you can work with a wide range of materials and there's the option of multi-colour printing.

There's also a built-in camera, so you can film timelapses of your print jobs and monitor in real time, and it has a self-clean function.

My exception to this recommendation would be if you specifically want to create detailed miniatures or character models, which require ultra-fine precision and a higher surface quality. For that, the best-value introduction is the Mars 5 Ultra.

#9013. designboom listens: yuri suzuki explores the many dimensions of sound

from childhood memories of watching mtv on betamax to punk records that clear his head, the london- and margate-based artist and designer shares the music behind a practice that turns listening into a physical and collective experience.

Yuri Suzuki uses sound as a material for shaping spaces, creating encounters, and bringing people together. His practice moves between sound, technology, sculpture, and graphic design, often inviting audiences to participate. Recent public commissions explore how artificial intelligence and machine learning can generate evolving sound environments, allowing each visitor to experience and contribute to a work in a different way. Accessibility is central to this approach: as Suzuki puts it, his projects aim to be ‘accessible to the many.’

Music follows a similarly open-ended logic in his own creative life. Asked which track best captures his practice, the Tokyo-born artist and designer, based between London and Margate, chooses Cornelius’ The Micro Disneycal World Tour, describing it as ‘a wonderful mixture of different musical elements, almost like a melting pot of sounds and ideas.’ He is drawn to its optimism and the way its complexity remains accessible, qualities he also tries to bring into his projects. Yuri Suzuki’s listening habits move between punk, electronic music, Japanese pop, and experimental sounds. Teengenerate and Melt-Banana help him clear his head when starting a project or working through a creative block, while Donald Fagen’s New Frontier takes him back to watching MTV recordings on Betamax as a child in Tokyo. His selections also reveal a longstanding interest in the relationship between music and objects, from the playful packaging of Mark Mothersbaugh’s limited-edition cassette to Peter Saville’s iconic sleeve design for New Order’s Blue Monday.

For designboom listens, Suzuki shares the tracks that accompany his creative process, the memories attached to particular songs, and the sounds he imagines alongside his own work. Read on for his selections and listen to the full playlist below.

What song best captures your creative practice?

Yuri Suzuki (YS): Cornelius — The Micro Disneycal World Tour. I think this track represents my creative practice quite well. It’s a wonderful mixture of different musical elements, almost like a melting pot of sounds and ideas. There’s a sense of optimism running through it, and despite its complexity, it feels very accessible and universal. I think these are qualities I also try to bring into my own projects.

What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?

YS: Teengenerate — My GTO. This is a difficult one, but I often find punk music is the best way to clear my head. Something loud, fast and direct helps wash away whatever I’ve been thinking about and gives me a fresh start. Teengenerate’s My GTO is perfect for that.

Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?

YS: Donald Fagen — New Frontier. My father had a Betamax videotape of MTV recordings, and this music video was on it. I remember watching it at night when I was in kindergarten. Even now, whenever I hear the song, I can immediately picture those evenings and the atmosphere of watching that video as a small child. I still listen to it quite often.

What song is stuck in your head right now?

YS: Happy End — Kaze wo Atsumete. When I was in Tokyo in August, I had the chance to meet Haruomi Hosono and have a lovely conversation with him. Perhaps because of that, I’ve found myself humming Kaze wo Atsumete by Happy End, the band he was part of in the early 1970s, quite a lot recently.

What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track, the one you secretly know every word to?

YS: Jeff Mills — Gamma Player / Mark Mothersbaugh — Musik for Insomniaks. Jeff Mills’ Gamma Player is one of my favorite things to listen to late at night. There’s something about hearing it in the middle of the night that feels absolutely wonderful.

Another favorite is Mark Mothersbaugh’s Musik for Insomniaks. As the title suggests, it’s a wonderful soundtrack for listening to in the middle of the night. It was also released on CD, but the limited-edition cassette version sold in Japan was particularly special. Not only did it have different content, but it also came with playing cards inside the package. I love the whole concept, both musically and as a physical object.

What song do you put on when you are stuck and need a breakthrough?

YS: Melt-Banana — Free the Bee. When I’m stuck, I tend to listen to punk or thrash metal. I like music with enough energy to completely blow away whatever is going on in my head. I often listen to Melt-Banana, and if I had to choose one track, it would be Free the Bee.

What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you are making right now?

YS: Buffalo Daughter — あ (AH). My friends in Buffalo Daughter released a new track called あ this week, so I’ve been listening to it a lot. It’s incredibly catchy and keeps playing in my head. I don’t know yet whether it’s influencing my work, but it’s certainly staying with me.

What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details?

YS: Róisín Murphy — Through Time. I love this track by Róisín Murphy, produced by my friend Matthew Herbert. It has such a beautiful melody and wonderful sonic textures. There’s something very calming about it, and it helps me slow down and pay attention to the smaller details in sound.

If people were to wear headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing?

YS: Raymond Scott — Portfolio 2. I think Raymond Scott’s Portfolio 2 would be a wonderful accompaniment to Onomatopia. His sound world feels very close to the kind of imaginary sonic environments suggested by the sculptures and their visual language. Although I have also composed my own soundtrack for the project, I think this would be a lovely alternative way to experience it.

YS: New Order — Blue Monday, designed by Peter Saville. I’ve always loved Peter Saville’s sleeve design for New Order’s Blue Monday. Inspired by an old floppy disk, the sleeve uses actual die-cut openings to recreate its appearance. Even the typography is replaced by a clever colour-coded system, adding another playful layer to the design. I love how it combines these little surprises with such a striking, minimal aesthetic. It’s playful, beautifully considered, and still looks incredibly cool.

What is a track that best describes your favourite project you have worked on so far?

YS: OK Go — Television, Television. I love all the projects I’ve worked on, so it’s difficult to choose just one. But one project that was particularly special was designing the record sleeve for OK Go’s album And the Adjacent Possible in 2025.

The sleeve opens to reveal an intricate three-dimensional pop-up sculpture, and the project received a Grammy nomination for Best Recording Package in 2026. The track I’ve chosen isn’t actually from that album. It’s Television, Television from their earlier record Oh No. I wanted to choose something by OK Go because I really enjoy their playful and experimental approach to music and visual ideas.

#9012. Nopales Benefits: Why You Might Add Cactus to Your Diet

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Looking at a cactus with its threatening spikes and tough skin, you might not immediately think, “Yep, that’s a thing I could eat.” But guess what? Some forms of cacti are edible, tasty, and quite good for you!

Check out why it might be a good idea to pal around with nopales, the pads of the prickly pear cactus.

The nopal cactus, also known as the prickly pear or the opuntia, is a shrub-like, flowering cactus native to parts of Mexico, Arizona, the Mediterranean, Australia, and other desert regions. It might be recognized by its multitude of connected pads with flowering blooms. (A pad in bloom looks a little like a flat, green paw.)

Nopales flowers are filled with a viscous, seeded substance often used in jams, jellies, pies, cakes, and other sweets. But the stems, leaves, and entire pad (with spines removed, obvs) are also edible. Traditional Mexican preparations include boiling, grilling, and sautéing.

Science is still examining the possible benefits of nopales, so some touted wellness perks are fairly tentative. Here’s a look at what we know about these desert fruits.

Almost any time you see bright colors in edible fruits, it’s a sign they contain antioxidants. This is def true for Nopales!

Older studies have found that the fruit inside their flowers is rich in antioxidants like ascorbic acid, phenolics, and a mixture of betacyanin and betaxanthin. These compounds help fight inflammation by kicking harmful free radicals out of your cells.

Since they combat inflammation, the antioxidants in prickly pear could improve joint mobility. In a 2020 study, people who drank 3 ounces of prickly pear juice daily for 8 weeks had better range of motion and greater ease with daily activities than a control group who drank a placebo.

Research suggests nopales may help steady blood sugar. A 2014 study found that people with type 2 diabetes who ate nopales with a high-carb breakfast had significantly lower blood sugar and insulin levels compared to those who didn’t. However, this study only included 14 participants.

In 2019, a larger systematic review assessed the fruit’s potential for blood sugar regulation. While it found insufficient evidence to support using nopales to reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, the authors noted it might significantly reduce blood glucose levels.

Showing your liver some love might involve adding nopales (or a glass of nopal juice) to your diet. According to research from 2023, this has to do with prickly pear’s effects on triglycerides. By helping reduce triglyceride accumulation, nopales could relieve stress on the liver.

Whether you’ve overdone it on booze or are down with a stomach bug, it’s important to rehydrate with a drink that contains electrolytes. Consider prickly pear juice as your back-on-the-wagon beverage. It’s got potassium, magnesium, and calcium to help rebalance your electrolyte levels.

If you can track down fresh nopales where you live, cooking it yourself is a fun (if somewhat complicated) way to take advantage of its benefits. If not, look for prickly pear products, such as juices, being sure to check for added sugars.

You can also take a supplement. Nopales supplements typically contain 500-650 milligrams (mg) per day.

While a prickly pear smoothie or nopales salad can be a healthy addition to your diet, consuming this cactus fruit may have some less-than-desirable side effects, like:

If you’re new to nopales, take it slow at first to see how your body responds.

Don’t let the “prickly” in prickly pear keep you away from this desert gem. When prepared correctly, nopales are unique, nutritious food. Check ’em out when your fruit basket needs something a little different.

#9011. Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, launched to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a big impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play

Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all users.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a company after that.”

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

“I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”

Lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on their architecture for migrant pregnant mothers. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” said Abascal.

“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

“Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a big issue and will be forever for these big cities.”

There is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

#9010. CAN combines eclectic references for eccentric revamp of London house

Towers of concrete drainage tubes and colourful exposed steel elements are among the eclectic features of House Tropicália, a “very personal” London residence recently extended by local architecture studio CAN.

Located in Catford, the project responds to a brief with “two distinct strands” – one relating to the functional elements of the project, and the other to its expressive and atmospheric qualities.

Functionally, CAN was asked to introduce a new kitchen and dining space that felt connected to the garden, alongside two new bedrooms on the first floor.

Meanwhile, the design was required to be an expression of the interests and experiences of its clients – designer Fabiane Lee-Perrella, television producer Robin Lee-Perrella and their two sons.

“The atmospheric side of the brief was to somehow encapsulate the clients’ diverse visual tastes and architectural memories from their pasts,” CAN founder Mat Barnes told Dezeen.

“This resulted in the eclecticism of the project; one that is very personal to the clients.”

Visual references given to CAN included modernist Brazilian architecture projects such as Lina Bo Bardi’s SESC Pompéia in São Paulo, as well as industrial architecture, David Hockney paintings and Moroccan riads.

The resultant design inspired the project’s name, House Tropicália, which nods to the late 1960s Tropicália movement that celebrated bold ideas and rebelled against accepted norms.

“We reject the idea that a project needs to be driven by a single, homogeneous idea or material,” said Barnes.

“Instead, we celebrate the complexity, diversity and even contradiction inherent in our clients’ tastes and design references,” he continued.

“We see these different influences not as competing ideas, but as an opportunity to create something individual and ultimately more meaningful.”

The focal point of the project is its highly unique rear elevation, with features including two towers of engineering drainage tubes, which break through a red-steel canopy that extends over the patio.

Meanwhile, bright blue and red fibre-cement panels decorate its elevation, alongside portions of textured raked render and exposed concrete, punctured by irregular shapes.

Details also include a metal sawtooth roof at first-floor level, alongside a bright yellow screen facing the neighbouring property to prevent overlooking.

Finally, at ground level, a full-width set of doors open onto a patio with a winding perimeter, referencing the designs of Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx.

“It brings together a mix of materials, forms and ideas drawn from the huge range of references the clients shared with us,” said Barnes. “I think it captures the character and personalities of the clients brilliantly.”

Inside, the back half of the ground floor has been rearranged to maximise its connection to the rear garden. This is where the new open-plan kitchen, dining and living space is positioned.

Meanwhile, at the front of the ground floor, the studio has created a secondary dining area and living space, and a children’s playroom in the original lounge.

Above, a void on the north side of the first floor has been filled to add a main bedroom suite, complete with an ensuite and roof terrace. Another bedroom has also been added.

The roof terrace has a walk-on, diamond-shaped skylight, which sits directly above the dining table.

Interior finishes echo the eclecticism of the exterior, with a bold mix of colours, materials and textures. This includes exposed steel joists and trusses, and a colourful timber kitchen with contrasting black tiles.

Walls of ceramic tiles on the ground floor have shell-like forms, handmade by Fabiane Lee-Perrella with glazing that shifts from pink to blue hues.

A microcement floor runs throughout the ground floor and incorporates pebble inlay that evokes a river and is a nod to the water feature at SESC Pompéia.

CAN hopes the project will highlight the importance of challenging the “established or standard way of doing things in a particular city or context”.

“We think it’s important to look beyond the usual architectural references and draw inspiration from unexpected places, whether that be sculpture, set design, or even infrastructure,” Barnes said.

“These disciplines can offer entirely different ways of thinking about space, material and form. Ultimately, it’s about exposing clients to these different ways of doing things.”

CAN, known fully as Critical Architecture Network, was founded by Barnes in 2016. Its previous projects include the equally bold house extensions Druid Grove and Mountain View.

#9009. Ultimate Guide to 4A Hair: Care Tips, Styles, and Maintenance

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Understanding your hair type is key to achieving healthy, luscious curls. Hair types range from 1 to 4 — straight, wavy, curly, and coily — with type 4 being the curliest. Type 4A hair has a fine texture and loose curl pattern, forming springy coils that need special care to stay healthy and vibrant.

Knowing your hair type helps determine the best hair care routine. Caring for 4A hair is essential, whether you’re dealing with dryness or breakage or want to define your curls.

Let’s dive into the world of 4A hair and discover how to keep those curls popping.

Alright, curl friends, let’s break it down. Hair type falls into four main categories:

Now, Type 4 hair is where things get seriously curly and coily. Within this category, we’ve got subtypes A, B, and C,

which refer to the width and density of your curls.

So, what’s the deal with 4A hair? 4A hair is the queen of the fine, loose curl pattern. It forms tight, springy coils that are like tiny, perfect S-shapes. These curls are less dense than their 4B and 4C cousins, making them more defined and delicate. Think of 4A hair as the Goldilocks of coily hair — not too tight, not too loose, but just right.

Your hair is unique and gorgeous, but it requires a bit of extra TLC to keep it looking its best. Here’s a straightforward guide to keeping your 4A hair moisturized, healthy, and thriving:

4A hair tends to be dry as its coily structure makes it difficult for natural oils to travel down the hair shaft. Keeping it moisturized is essential, so incorporate a good leave-in conditioner into your daily shampooing routine. Use deep conditioning treatments weekly to replenish moisture and strengthen your curls.

Don’t forget scalp care, too! For maximum hydration, look for products with ingredients like shea butter, coconut oil, and glycerin.

4A hair is prone to tangles, so detangle gently to avoid breakage. Use a wide-tooth comb or your fingers to work through knots carefully. Start from the ends and work your way up to the roots, and always detangle when your hair is wet and coated with conditioner to provide slip and minimize damage.

Heat styling tools can cause significant damage to 4A hair, leading to dryness, breakage, and loss of curl pattern. Minimize the use of blow dryers, flat irons, and curling wands. If you use heat, always apply a heat protectant spray first to shield your hair from high temperatures.

Pro tip: To maintain the health of your curls, opt for air-drying or styles that don’t require heat.

Protective styles like braids, twists, and buns can help reduce manipulation and minimize breakage. These styles tuck away your ends, protecting them from friction and environmental damage.

Cotton pillowcases cause friction, which leads to frizz and breakage, especially for 4A hair. Switching to satin or silk pillowcases instead helps mai

ntain your curl pattern and prevent tangles.

Regular trims are crucial for keeping 4A hair healthy and preventing split ends from traveling up the hair shaft. Aim to trim your hair every 8-12 weeks to remove damaged ends and keep your curls looking fresh and vibrant.

Yes, 4A hair is curly and falls under the coily category. It features tight, springy curls that form an S-shape.

To determine your hair type, look at the curl pattern, texture, and density. 4A hair has a loose curl pattern with fine, springy coils, while 4B and 4C hair have tighter curls. 3C hair is curly but not as tight as Type 4.

Washing once a week or every two weeks is generally sufficient for 4A hair. Overwashing can strip the hair of its natural oils.

Regular trims every 8-12 weeks help keep 4A hair healthy by removing split ends and preventing breakage.

Taking care of your 4A hair isn’t rocket science, but it does need a little know-how and the right tools.

Love those natural curls — keep them hydrated, avoid excessive heat, and give them some nighttime TLC.

#9008. human point frames architecture as an unfolding timeline

in conversation with designboom, human point founder loukas fotopoulos reveals how the practice choreographs architecture, development and construction around human movement, connection and experience.

mariana rodrigues November 25, 2026 9 min

With three decades of practice behind it, Human Point approaches the built environment as a living sequence shaped by human presence. Spanning architecture, urban planning, real estate development, investment strategy, engineering, and turn-key construction, the multidisciplinary practice integrates architectural vision, technical expertise, and economic thinking into a unified approach, from initial concept to completed development.

In a recent conversation with designboom, founder Loukas Fotopoulos unpacks how this directorial lens shapes the practice, treating physical space as a fluid timeline that unfolds through shifting light, evolving perspectives, and tactile materiality. This framework casts residents as active protagonists whose movement and interactions bring each environment to life in real time.

Loukas Fotopoulos established his own architectural practice in 1996, continuing a family tradition of architecture. Having grown up alongside his father, architect Eleftherios Fotopoulos, in his architectural studio, he developed an early understanding of architectural thinking and practice. In 2008, his practice evolved into Human Point, expanding its approach beyond architecture.

Across residential, hospitality, and urban scales, the studio brings architecture, strategic development consulting, and immersive visual communication under one roof. Inside this open laboratory of ideas, every phase takes shape through continuous dialogue between creators and inhabitants.

Human Point began as an architectural practice in 1996. How has it evolved?

Loukas Fotopoulos (LF): Architecture remains the foundation of everything we do. But over time, I became increasingly interested in everything that determines whether a good architectural idea becomes a good building. Design is one part of a larger process involving land, feasibility, planning, engineering, construction, financing and, ultimately, how people experience the completed project. Human Point evolved to bring these decisions together, from the earliest investment strategy through construction. We wanted to take responsibility for the entire process rather than simply contribute to one stage. For me, this is not about offering more services. It is about protecting the coherence of the original idea.

You are both an architect and a filmmaker. How does cinema influence your architecture?

(LF): Architecture is often represented through static images, although nobody experiences a building that way. We move through space in time. Light changes, views unfold, materials approach the body. There is anticipation, transition and sometimes surprise. Cinema taught me to think in sequences. In architecture, the person inhabiting the space becomes the protagonist. There is another connection. Before directing a character, you must understand that character and, in a way, love them. Architecture requires something similar. Before designing for people, you must be genuinely interested in them. An architect, particularly one involved in development, cannot remain isolated in a studio. You need to understand society, economics, politics, science, technology and culture. And you need to enjoy life: travel, meet people, observe, celebrate and sometimes simply have fun. If architecture creates places for life, you must remain curious about life itself. That curiosity often generates unexpected, playful ideas that can also carry social purpose and economic intelligence.

What does human-centered architecture mean in practice?

Development is increasingly criticized for its impact on cities, islands and communities. Can development genuinely be human-centered?

(LF): Absolutely, but not automatically. Development becomes problematic when short-term financial return is its only criterion. Yet development itself is essential. We need investment, housing, hospitality, infrastructure and the intelligent transformation of existing buildings. The question is how we do it. A carefully studied development can respect its location, respond to real needs, use resources intelligently and remain economically successful. I don’t believe architecture has to choose between human value and economic value. Good development should create both. Capital is essential, but it should work alongside architectural vision, scientific knowledge, technical expertise, social responsibility and long-term thinking.

And meaningful development opportunities should not necessarily belong only to large institutional players.

Private investors, smaller investment groups and landowners should also be able to participate in professionally structured developments when they have access to the appropriate architectural, financial and technical expertise. For that to happen, the institutional and regulatory framework should provide fair and equal conditions for participation, regardless of scale. In a sense, this is also a political position. Not against capital — we need capital and want to work with it — but in favor of profitable investment that recognizes wider social, environmental and cultural responsibilities. Private value and collective benefit do not always have to be in conflict. In fact, well-conceived development can strengthen both.

Where did your interest in the economics of architecture begin?

(LF): During the Greek financial crisis, I began exploring how architecture could generate economic as well as spatial value. This led to House Income, a European-funded research project investigating income-generating buildings. Farm Stories in Syros developed this idea, combining architecture, agritourism, renewable energy and hospitality into a productive economy, inspired by traditional Greek island households where home, land and livelihood were interconnected. We wanted to reinterpret that intelligence for contemporary life. The relationship between architecture, sustainability and economic resilience continues to shape our approach to development.

Why did Human Point begin developing its own projects?

(LF): After years of designing, advising and managing construction for others, we wanted to test our ideas directly, with our own resources and responsibility. Whispering Elia in Mykonos gave us that opportunity. Its earth-sheltered villas become part of the steep Cycladic terrain rather than objects placed upon it. By investing our own capital and work, we are testing whether uncompromising architecture and commercially sustainable development can genuinely coexist. Whispering Ampeli in Kefalonia explores another relationship with landscape, drawing on historic vineyard terraces, vegetation and views towards the Ionian Sea.

In Voula, we are developing a premium residence organized around a sunlit vertical atrium, greenery and a continuous dialogue between interior and exterior space. Shapes Ermoupolis in Syros demonstrates this approach. We presented a private investor with our vision for transforming a severely damaged listed building into a boutique hotel. He trusted our proposal, and together we brought it to life. The project delivered strong financial returns while preserving architectural heritage, revitalizing the waterfront and creating employment. It shows how private capital and architectural expertise can generate economic, social, cultural and environmental value together. For me, commercial viability should be a design parameter, not an obstacle to good architecture.

Does transforming existing buildings represent another form of development?

(LF): Certainly. Development does not always mean building something new. In Vouliagmeni, we are transforming an existing five-storey residential structure into three premium residences through new spatial configurations, pools, landscape, generous openings and a new architectural identity, while retaining much of its structural framework. This is also value creation: understanding what already exists and discovering how architecture can unlock its potential rather than automatically replacing it.

Your projects vary dramatically. Is there a common architectural language?

(LF): I hope there is a common way of thinking rather than a recognizable style. At the Riviera Tower Penthouse in Ellinikon, we are working with bespoke interiors, art, technology and materials in an exceptional urban setting. In Mykonos, architecture almost disappears into the earth. In Vouliagmeni, an existing structure acquires a new identity. In Syros, architecture can become part of a productive landscape or revive a historic building. The visual results are different, but the questions remain: Who is this for? How should it feel? What does the location demand? What is necessary, and what is unnecessary? How can the project create lasting value?I am more interested in consistency of thought than consistency of appearance.

After thirty years, what do you want Human Point to become?

(LF): I want it to remain boutique. And maybe win an Oscar one day. Human Point should be large enough to unite architecture, engineering, development, investment strategy and construction, yet small enough for every important project to matter to us personally. Ultimately, we want to create architectural, human, environmental, social and economic value together. When these values coexist, architecture and development become part of the same idea — and, hopefully, one worth loving.

projects:  Whispering Elia, Mykonos Greece

Whispering Ampeli, Assos, Kefalonia, Greece

Riviera Tower Penthouse, Ellinikon, Athens Greece

Vouliagmeni Premium Residential Building, Athens Riviera, Greece

Voula Residence, Premium Private Residence, Athens Riviera, Greece

#9007. Atelier Manferdini uses digital glitches to shape tile-and-metal facade of Virginia power station

Photography by Dave Huh unless stated

California-based studio Atelier Manferdini has created an expressive facade system for an electrical substation in Virginia, USA, using metal and colourful tile to represent the flow of electrical power within.

Called InVisible, the project was carried out for Dominion Energy, an electricity provider that was updating the substation in Crystal City, Northern Virginia, just outside of Washington DC.

Atelier Manferdini founder Elena Manferdini, who is Italian and teaches at Sci-Arc in Los Angeles, said that her studio sought to translate the largely functional structure into something more human.

“Critical infrastructure is essential to our cities, yet the Dominion Energy substation is fundamentally designed for machines rather than people,” Manferdini told Dezeen.

“With inVisible, we wanted to explore this dichotomy, transforming a purely functional structure into something meaningful to the surrounding community,” she continued.

“While the interior responds to the needs of machines, the exterior becomes an opportunity to engage with people through color, pattern, and perception, creating a dialogue between infrastructure and the human scale of the city.”

The substation converts power into different voltages to facilitate the transmission of energy, and the patterns on the sculptural facade were computationally designed to represent that process.

Atelier Manferdini used programming site Processing, which came out of the MIT Media Lab in the early 2000s, to design the colourful tile band that lines the bottom of the structure.

This pattern incorporates 10 colours and tiles of three different sizes, two, four, and six inches across – a reference to voltages – along with “glitches” in the program to create the graphic.

It recalls the Boogie Woogie works of modernist artist Piet Mondrian, which were based on the rhythms of cities.

Above the ceramic pattern, the studio placed massive gridded aluminium panels.

The panels create a ventilated facade system, set at different distances from the exterior walls and stacked where they meet so that sunlight passes through different densities in the gridded pattern, creating a variable light effect.

“The folds catch light and cast shadows, allowing the surface to shift with the time of day and the viewer’s position,” said the studio.

At night, the panels are backlit by programmable LEDs.

Overall, the studio said that it considers the contrast between the monochromatic metal and colour tile patterns a unified image.

“Quiet and metallic above, saturated and granular below, the two bands form a unified architectural composition,” said the studio, with the unseen machines humming with electricity inside.

Other creative takes on infrastructure include a power station in China that Schmidt Hammer Lassen shrouded with steel lamellas and topped with a walkway, as well as a sculptural stormwater facility in Toronto by GH3, a Canadian studio well known for its aesthetic treatment of otherwise overlooked infrastructure.

#9006. Pucker Up! How to Heal Cracked Lip Corners Fast

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Smiling for selfies should be fun, not painful! If cracked lip corners or angular cheilitis make it hard to smile, eat, or kiss, don’t worry. Check out these tips to heal those cracks quickly. With some care and good habits, you’ll have pain-free, makeout-ready lips in no time. Say goodbye to angular cheilitis and hello to a happier smile!

The first step to healing your cracked lip corners quickly is to lock in any moisture. Reach for a product dermatologists call an occlusive, which creates a protective barrier that prevents your lip corners from getting drier. Vaseline, Aquafor, or CeraVe ointment are common occlusives that will help reduce cracking.

Dab a little coconut oil, olive oil, or fragrance-free moisturizer on the corners of your lips daily after you shower. Make it a daily habit, but don’t go overboard. A little dab will do. Allow your skin’s natural oils to build back up as the cracking fades. Bonus tip: Add the occlusive lip barrier after moisturizing.

Locking in moisture only works if you have enough moisture, so staying hydrated is key! Keep a refillable water bottle with you as your trusty sidekick. Sip on plain water throughout the day, or jazz it up with a splash of cucumber or another non-acidic flavor. Pro tip: Avoid lemon juice, which can irritate and sting sensitive skin.

Bonus: Staying hydrated will help your raw lip corners heal quicker and improve your skin’s overall health.

Have you noticed that moisture is a common theme here? Lend your lips a humid hand by sleeping with a humidifier beside your bed. Adding moisture to the air is especially helpful for your cracked lips during the winter or in hot, dry climates. Think about popping a small humidifier in your workspace or wherever you spend the most time.

It might seem like a quick fix to lick your lips to keep them moist, but that can make things worse. Saliva evaporates quickly, leaving a sticky residue that can attract bacteria and lead to infection. So, keep your tongue away from your lips and remember this: “Licking your lips will cause them to lickety-split.”

Whether from frigid cold or dry heat, your skin can lose water rapidly, causing cracking, flaking, discoloration, or swelling. So avoid jumping from a sweltering afternoon at the beach into a freezing cold movie theater.

Also, skip the hot showers or cold plunges for a bit. These types of rapid temperature changes will quickly dry out your lip corners. Bonus tip: Your lips can take a beating from the sun, so find a lip balm with SPF protection.

If your cracked lip corners don’t improve or become especially painful or swollen in a few days, it’s time to visit a board-certified dermatologist. If left untreated, angular cheilitis can last for years, leaving your lips discolored or scarred.

FYI: Angular cheilitis might not appear as clearly in people with darker skin. Instead of turning red, the affected skin may look pale and have a darker border.

Remember that lickety-split mantra? It’s for real. Saliva can get deposited in the corners of your lips for many reasons, like drooling, smoking, or sleeping with your mouth open due to some sniffles. Bacteria grows in those little saliva pools, triggering an inflammatory response that causes your lip corners to get irritated and crack.

Following these tips will make your lips feel better in about a week. Really bad cases of angular cheilitis can take a few weeks. Avoid smoking and eat a balanced diet to get faster results.

As mentioned above, Vaseline and other occlusives help create a protective barrier over the cracked lip corners, which helps the healing process.

You might have woken up with cracked lip corners, but you won’t be able to get rid of them overnight. Be patient and follow the tips above!

Say goodbye to painful cracked lip corners in about a week with these easy tips:

Talk to a dermatologist for customized care if your lip corners become red, swollen, or more painful after a few days.

#9005. nick cave and india pavilion win the visitors’ lions at the venice art biennale 2026

following the resignation of the international jury, this year’s biennale gives audiences a direct role in deciding which artists and national presentations receive recognition.

The public has selected its favorites at the 61st Venice Art Biennale, with American artist Nick Cave receiving the Visitors’ Lion for Best Participant and India winning Best National Participation for its pavilion, Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home. Announced by La Biennale di Venezia on November 25th, 2026, the awards reflect the preferences of visitors to In Minor Keys, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh.

Following the resignation of the International Jury, the institution introduced two Visitors’ Lions, inviting audiences to vote for the Best Participant in In Minor Keys and the Best National Participation throughout the exhibition. The decision placed public engagement at the center of this year’s awards, giving visitors a direct role in determining which artistic presentations received recognition.

Born in Chicago in 1959, Cave receives the recognition for his participation in the main exhibition. Working across sculpture, performance, textiles, and installation, the artist has developed a practice that explores identity, material culture, race, and the possibilities of transformation. His work frequently brings together elaborate material compositions and performative gestures, creating spaces where art becomes an encounter between the body, movement, and collective experience.

India’s winning national participation brings together five artists: Alwar Balasubramaniam, Sumakshi Singh, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, and Skarma Sonam Tashi. Commissioned by the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), Ministry of Culture, and curated by Amin Jaffer, the presentation occupied the Arsenale. Its title frames the exhibition around questions of distance and belonging, placing the idea of home at the center of a collective artistic presentation.
