#8973. Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Building muscle on a vegetarian diet isn’t rocket science, but it requires some know-how. Here are some tips to keep you on track.

In other words, aim for 0.73 to 1 gram per pound of body weight per day. For example, if you weigh 150 pounds, this would mean you should consume about 110 to 150 grams of protein each day.

For optimal muscle growth, it’s not just the total amount of protein you consume daily that matters but also how you distribute it throughout the day. To best support muscle growth and repair, aim to consume protein at each meal and snack, roughly every 3–4 hours. #8971. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

#8969. HTA Design unveils "UK's largest council housing development"

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

#8968. Rucking Benefits: Add Weight to Your Walk to Boost Fitness and Strength

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Weightlifting isn’t the only way to build muscle. Rucking, or walking with a weighted backpack, is also highly effective. It’s easy to start, can be done anywhere, and helps build muscle, burn fat, and boost endurance.

Curious? Keep reading to discover why rucking might become your new favorite workout!

Rucking is like taking your regular walk and cranking up the intensity with heavy cargo. It’s as simple as strapping on a weighted backpack (aka rucksack) and hitting the pavement, the trail, or wherever you like to roam. Originally dreamed up by the military to toughen up soldiers, rucking, or a rucksack march has, er, marched into civilian life as a killer workout.

What makes it awesome? The extra weight transforms a casual stroll into a workout that means business. Plus, it’s customizable — you can load up as much or as little weight as you want, making it perfect for any fitness level. And the best part is that you can ruck just about anywhere.

Rucking isn’t just a walk in the park — it’s a powerful workout that packs a punch in all the right places. Here’s why rucking deserves a spot in your fitness routine:

Think of rucking as the ultimate multitasker for your body. It’s like lifting weights but with cardio to keep your heart pumping.

As you lug that weighted backpack around, your legs, back, and core are putting in serious work, building strength, and endurance with every (weighted) step.

Want to torch calories without the treadmill monotony? Rucking’s got you covered. The extra weight and steady movement combo turns your stroll into a calorie-burning machine. Perfect for shedding any additional pounds while keeping things interesting.

Carrying a weighted backpack helps your posture. Your core has to stay engaged to keep you balanced, which helps align your body and ward off injury.

If you’ve had a baby, rucking can be a game-changer, helping combat the postural shifts of pregnancy and hauling around kids. Plus, it builds the functional strength you need for everyday life, like lifting groceries or wrangling toddlers.

Rucking easily fits into a busy schedule. You don’t need special equipment beyond a sturdy backpack or a gym membership, and you can do it while multitasking — think walking the dog in the morning or pushing a stroller. Plus, the whole family can join in, making it a great way to combine fitness with family time.

Starting rucking is easy, but here are some tips to help you get the most out of your rucks:

Rucking is generally safe, but here’s how to stay injury-free:

Yes, rucking can help build muscle, especially in your legs, core, and back. The added weight provides resistance, similar to strength training.

Start with 10 to 15% of your body weight and adjust based on your comfort and fitness level. Heavier weights can affect your balance and stance, making injuries more likely. As you progress, you can gradually increase the weight.

Yes. Rucking forces your upper back and shoulder muscles to step up, giving your traps a solid workout as you carry the weight.

Ruck yes! Rucking is a low-impact, full-body workout that kicks butt.

Tell your boring walk on the treadmill to ruck off and trade it in for a waltz about with a weighted rucksack. Rucking could be the secret sauce your fitness routine has been missing, helping you build muscle, shed pounds, or get those steps in.

#8967. Japanese Perspectives

Japanese Perspectives, published by Distanz Verlag, Berlin, explores architectural responses to resource scarcity, demographic change, and climate adaptation through the lens of contemporary Japan.Bringing together essays by Japanese architects, selected projects and observations from everyday urban life, the book examines practices of reuse, transformation, and working with existing structures.The contributions reveal an architectural culture in which tradition and innovation, continuity and change, are continuously negotiated—inviting a reconsideration of architecture as a cultural practice of adaptation and renewal.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

#8964. Why Does My Side Hurt When I Run? Causes and Prevention Tips

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

This pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod says tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

This common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

According to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a big race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

When a side stitch strikes, don’t stress – there are steps you can take, including:

To stop a side stitch before it begins, here are some ideas FTW:

Side stitches are usually harmless. But it’s always a good idea to visit a pro if you experience any of the following probs:

Side stitches are a common issue and not typically the reason for concern. Though pros don’t know what causes them, they think issues with breathing, posture, or nerves may play a role.

Consider working on your running form or breathing to reduce the risk of experiencing a side stitch. Staying hydrated and avoiding huge meals pre-run may also help. Consider working with a physical therapist or personal trainer if your issues persist.

If you experience pain under your breastbone when running, visit a doctor asap.

#8962. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen says. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”

#8961. Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice New-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth

#8960. Fenix Art Museum / MAD Architects

Text description provided by the architects. Fenix is a major new museum that explores migration through the lens of art, opening on a landmark site in Rotterdam's City Harbor, developed by internationally acclaimed architects MAD. With a rapidly expanding collection of historic and contemporary objects, Fenix tells the story of migration through a series of encounters with art, architecture, photography, food, and history. Located in what was once part of the world's largest transshipment warehouse, on a peninsula in Rotterdam's historic port district, Fenix overlooks the docks where millions of migrant journeys began and ended. The monumental 16,000 square meter warehouse has been transformed to become Fenix by MAD Architects with restoration consultation by Bureau Polderman. This is MAD Architects' first commission for a public cultural building in Europe, as well as the first museum to be built by a Chinese firm in Europe. The project was initiated by the Droom en Daad Foundation, founded in 2016. The Foundation is helping redefine Rotterdam for the 21st century - developing new kinds of arts and culture institutions and fostering new creative talent that reflects the city's diversity, its spirit, and its history

#8959. Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

“Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik says. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

“Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

The steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”

Still, it’s important to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she says.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

Both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

But if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s important to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

“Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

#8958. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#8956. Architects and designers celebrate at Dezeen Awards 2026 party in London

Photography by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

The British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be announced were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

Interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

All Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The next edition of Dezeen Awards will open in February 2027. Sign up for the Dezeen Awards newsletter to be the first to hear the latest updates.

The photography is by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.
